Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology: Lettrism, Alchemy, and the Secrets of the Letters in Medieval Islam.* Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism.* 2023.

concepts.name: Barzakh
concepts.card: **Al-Barzakh** (the Isthmus). In Ibn Turka's system, the intermediate realm between pure matter and pure spirit, between multiplicity and unity. The domain where letters become forms, where [[divine-names]] manifest as causal powers, where mathematics governs physical existence. Central to understanding how lettrism operates—letters do not merely represent reality but constitute the barzakh through which divine principles become concrete.
concepts.body:
## Al-Barzakh: The Intermediate Realm

**Al-Barzakh** (literally, "isthmus" or "barrier") is Ibn Turka's term for the ontological middle ground between pure spirit and pure matter. Qur'anically, the barzakh refers to the barrier between the two seas that prevents them from mixing. Medieval Islamic philosophers, especially Ibn ʿArabī, adopted this to denote the intermediate realm between intellect and sense, between the divine and the created. Ibn Turka transformed this concept into the centerpiece of his metaphysical system.

In Ibn Turka's framework, the Barzakh is not merely a philosophical abstraction but the **actual location where causation operates**. The barzakh is where [[ilm-al-huruf|letters and their numerical values]] exert power. It is the realm in which:

- Divine names (*asmaʾ*) become manifest in forms (*ashkāl*)
- Letters (*hurūf*) function as operative principles
- Mathematics (abjad numerology) governs the unfolding of creation
- Intention (*niyyah*) plus ritual acts produce concrete effects

Understanding the barzakh is essential for understanding how Ibn Turka reconciles rational philosophy with operative magic. Operations that recombine letters work not through mystical intuition but through precise knowledge of how the barzakh functions as the intermediate domain where formal patterns (mathematical, linguistic, geometric) generate effects in material reality.

The barzakh is also the human soul—Ibn Turka argues that human consciousness and will operate in the barzakh, which is why knowledge of letters and divine names grants operative power. Mastery of lettrist science is mastery of the mechanisms by which barzakh-realm knowledge becomes action.

## Where it sits in the hierarchy

The barzakh is defined by its position, so the levels either side of it are part of its definition. Creation is ordered as intelligible, imaginal and sensible: divine names in their unmanifested essence; subtle forms; material existence. The barzakh is the middle term, and the traffic between the outer two has to pass through it.

This is why it carries the operative weight. A cosmology of graded levels alone would describe how being descends. Ibn Turka's addition is that the descent has a **place where it can be worked** — that formal patterns introduced at the intermediate level propagate outward into the sensible one. The hierarchy explains the world; the barzakh is where a practitioner gets a hand on it. See also [[imaginal-realm|the imaginal realm]], which is [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī's]] name for substantially the same domain.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The barzakh is Ibn Turka's foundational cosmological concept; all occult operations depend on understanding it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 150-180.

concepts.name: Abjad numerology
concepts.card: **Abjad numerology** (Hisab al-Jumul). The system assigning numerical values to Arabic letters (alif=1, bāʾ=2, etc.), allowing letters and words to be manipulated mathematically. Central to [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]: Ibn Turka used abjad values to establish correspondences between divine names, cosmic principles, and human faculties. Enables the calculation of ''operative words'' whose numerical sum aligns with specific celestial or talismanic purposes.
concepts.body:
## Abjad Numerology (Hisab al-Jumul)

The **abjad system** is an ancient method of letter-to-number correspondence in Arabic and Hebrew. Each of the 28 Arabic letters carries a numerical value:
- alif (a) = 1, bāʾ (b) = 2, jīm (j) = 3... up to ghīn (gh) = 1000

This allowed Arabic letters, words, and verses to be treated as mathematical entities. The sum of a word's letters yields a number; that number can be matched against cosmic cycles, divine names, or talismanic intent.

In Ibn Turka's system, abjad numerology becomes **the bridge between language and mathematics, between expression and causation**. By selecting or composing words whose abjad sum equals a specific number—say, the number corresponding to the planet Venus or to a particular divine name—one creates a linguistic-mathematical object that resonates with that principle. Written or chanted correctly, such a word becomes operative.

Example: the divine name al-ʿAlīm ("the All-Knowing") has a specific abjad value. A talisman inscribed with a word or phrase whose abjad value matches that of al-ʿAlīm would, in theory, embody the properties of divine knowledge and could be used to attract or enhance that quality.

Ibn Turka's genius was systematizing abjad manipulation into a rigorous science rather than leaving it as scattered numerological tricks. He showed how abjad calculations, combined with proper understanding of the barzakh and divine names, provide a methodology for intentional causation grounded in cosmic principles.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Abjad is one of the core technical tools of [[ilm-al-huruf]]; mastery of it is necessary for operative lettrism.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, pp. 95-130. Ibn Turka, *Kitab al-Mafahis*, Chapters on Numerology.

concepts.name: The Divine Names
concepts.card: **Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya** (The Divine Names and Attributes). Islamic doctrine positing 28 (or 99) divine names—each expressing an aspect of God's nature (The Merciful, The Just, The Mighty, etc.). In [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], each of the 28 Arabic letters corresponds to one divine name, making letters themselves expressions of divine attributes. Ibn Turka's system treats mastery of the divine names through their corresponding letters as the path to aligning human will with cosmic principles.
concepts.body:
## The Divine Names (Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya)

Islamic theology recognizes that God is known through His attributes and names. The Qur'an references divine names, and Islamic scholars compiled lists—commonly 99, though sometimes 28. Each name expresses a dimension of divinity: al-Raḥmān (The Merciful), al-ʿAdl (The Just), al-ʿAlīm (The All-Knowing), al-Qawī (The Mighty), etc.

In [[ilm-al-huruf|Ibn Turka's lettrist system]], the 28 divine names are mapped directly onto the 28 Arabic letters. This creates a correspondence where:
- Each letter IS a divine name
- Each letter carries the properties and powers of that name
- Manipulation of letters becomes invocation of divine principles

For example:
- The letter ʿAyn corresponds to al-ʿAlīm (The All-Knowing)
- The letter Tāʾ corresponds to al-Tāʾib (The Returning/Repenting)
- The letter Qāf corresponds to al-Qawī (The Mighty)

Through understanding these correspondences and using [[abjad-numerology|abjad numerology]], a practitioner can compose words, phrases, or talismans that embody specific divine qualities. The goal is not manipulation (in the magical sense) but **attunement**: aligning human intention and action with divine attributes, thereby participating in the structure of reality itself.

Ibn Turka's treatment of the divine names through letters represents a synthesis of Islamic theology, [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist gnosis]], and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]]. It is the theological foundation that legitimizes lettrism as a valid science within Islamic orthodoxy—because engaging with letters is, from this perspective, engaging with divine attributes themselves.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The divine names are the theological anchor for [[ilm-al-huruf]]; they ground lettrist practice within Islamic doctrine.
literature: Ibn ʿArabī. *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya*, Treatise on the Divine Names.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, Ch. 3.

concepts.name: Pythagorean Cosmology
concepts.card: **Pythagorean Cosmology**. The ancient Greek doctrine that numbers and their ratios are the fundamental principles governing reality. Ibn Turka's distinctive contribution was grounding Islamic [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] explicitly in Pythagorean mathematics, arguing that letters and their [[abjad-numerology|numerical values]] encode cosmic principles just as Pythagoras taught that mathematics is the language of creation. This synthesis gave Islamic lettrism mathematical legitimacy and positioned it as a **truly universal science** encompassing reason, mysticism, and operative power.
concepts.body:
## Pythagorean Cosmology in Islamic Context

Pythagorean philosophy (c. 580–500 BCE) teaches that numbers are the fundamental constituents of reality. Numbers, through their ratios and relationships, generate harmony, order, and all manifestation. This worldview emphasizes that the cosmos is knowable through mathematics, and that mathematical knowledge grants insight into (and potentially influence over) the structure of creation.

The late-antique Neoplatonic tradition preserved and developed Pythagorean thought, eventually reaching the Islamic world through Hellenistic texts, Byzantine commentaries, and the writings of Islamic philosophers like al-Kindī and al-Fārābī. Yet lettrism in the Islamic world developed largely independently, growing from Qur'anic exegesis and gnosis without explicit Pythagorean framing.

### Ibn Turka's Innovation

Ibn Turka's genius was **explicitly connecting Islamic lettrism with Pythagorean principles**. He argued that:

1. **Letters are numbers**: Each of the 28 Arabic letters has a numerical value ([[abjad-numerology|abjad]])
2. **Numbers are cosmic**: Pythagorean mathematics describes the structure of creation
3. **Therefore, letters ARE cosmic principles**: Mastery of letters is mastery of the mathematics of creation

This move was philosophically powerful: it gave lettrism a pedigree reaching back to ancient Greece; it grounded it in mathematical reason rather than mystical intuition alone; and it positioned it as **the supreme science**, encompassing both rational (Pythagorean math) and mystical (gnostic lettrism) approaches.

By adopting the Pythagorean framework, Ibn Turka essentially reinvented lettrism as a **Neopythagorean system**—and in doing so, positioned Islamic occult philosophy as a genuine alternative universal science, rivaling and arguably exceeding the philosophical systems of contemporary Renaissance Europe.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Pythagorean cosmology is Ibn Turka's foundational theoretical framework; it structures his entire philosophical system.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography*.

concepts.name: The Imaginal Realm
concepts.literal_meaning: The realm of forms; the world of imagination
concepts.card: **Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl** (The Imaginal Realm). In [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysics, the ontological layer between pure intellect and material sense where forms (*ashkāl*) exist independently of physical matter. The domain where mystical visions occur, where symbols manifest, where divine names express themselves in subtle forms. Central to understanding how knowledge operates in Islamic mysticism and occultism: the imaginal realm is where letters and divine names acquire form, where talismanic operations work, where the barzakh functions.
concepts.body:
## Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl: The Imaginal Realm

**Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl** (literally "the imaginal realm" or "the realm of imagination") is [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] term for an intermediate ontological domain between pure intellect (ʿaql) and material sensation (ḥiss). The Arabic word *khiyāl* is often mistranslated as "imagination" in the modern sense (the faculty of fantasy); Ibn Arabi means something far more precise and metaphysically serious: a realm of subtle forms (*ashkāl*) that possess reality independent of physical matter.

The imaginal realm occupies the same position in Ibn Arabi's cosmology that the [[barzakh|barzakh]] occupies in Ibn Turka's refinement of it: the crucial intermediate domain where causation operates, where divine principles become manifest in form, where knowledge acquires structure.

### Three Realms of Being

Ibn Arabi divides creation into three principal domains:

1. **The Intelligible Realm** (*ʿālam al-ʿaql*): Pure intellect, transcendent principles, divine names in their unmanifested essence
2. **The Imaginal Realm** (*ʿālam al-khiyāl*): Forms, symbols, subtle bodies, the world of vision and mystical knowledge
3. **The Sensible Realm** (*ʿālam al-ḥiss*): Material existence, the physical world knowable through sense perception

Each realm participates in the others; none is hermetically sealed. The imaginal realm serves as the *medium* through which the intelligible becomes sensible, through which the transcendent becomes immanent.

### The Imaginal in Mystical Experience

For Ibn Arabi, mystical visions (*mushāhadāt*) are not hallucinations or mere psychological phenomena—they are direct perception of the imaginal realm. When a mystic "sees" an angel, perceives a divine light, or encounters a teacher in a dream, they are perceiving realities that exist in the imaginal realm. These perceptions are as real as sensory experience, though they operate in a different ontological register.

This doctrine revolutionizes Islamic mysticism: it legitimizes mystical experience as a form of genuine knowledge by establishing that there is an objective realm (the imaginal) in which such experiences occur. Mysticism is not projection; it is perception.

### The Imaginal in Occult Practice

[[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] and the later occult philosophers adopted this framework. When a practitioner creates a talisman by writing letters and numbers with specific intention, the operation works in the imaginal realm first: the talisman, as an imaginal object (a form constituted by [[abjad-numerology|numerical correspondences]] and divine names), exerts influence on the sensible world. The imaginal realm is where the power resides; the physical talisman is the expression.

Similarly, [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist operations]] work because letters—as forms carrying [[divine-names|divine names]]—are primarily imaginal realities. Mastery of letters grants access to the imaginal realm, whence all material creation flows.

### Legacy and Transmission

[[qunavi|Qūnavī]] elaborated Ibn Arabi's doctrine of the imaginal realm into a full philosophy of knowledge (*gnosis* vs. *reason*). Through the [[qunavi|Qūnavī]]-Jandī school, the imaginal realm became part of the theoretical apparatus available to philosophers, mystics, and occultists across the Islamic world. By Ibn Turka's time, the imaginal realm was accepted as a foundational concept: its reality was presupposed, not debated.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The imaginal realm is Ibn Arabi's key metaphysical contribution; all later Islamic occultism presupposes it.
literature: Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Imaginal Ontology and the New Brethren of Purity*.

concepts.name: Talismanic Science
concepts.card: **ilm al-Talasim** (Talismanic Science). Operative practice of creating talismans inscribed with letters, numbers, divine names. Based on theory that letters, numerical correspondences, and divine names are cosmic principles that, combined correctly with proper intention, exert force through intermediate realm. Central practical application of Ibn Turka's system.
concepts.body: **Talismanic science** (ilm al-talasim) is the operative discipline of creating objects—rings, seals, parchments, metals—inscribed with carefully chosen letters, numbers, and divine names to accomplish specific aims. Unlike superstition, talismanic science in Ibn Turka's systematization is grounded in rigorous cosmological theory. A talisman works: (1) Each 28 Arabic letter corresponds to divine name and cosmic power. (2) Combining letters by numerical correspondence (*abjad*) aligns word with specific principle (Venus, al-Alim, etc.). (3) Inscribing this word-object on appropriate matter with proper intention embodies the principle. (4) Through intermediate realm, talismanic object exerts influence—attracting love, granting wisdom, protecting. Creating talisman requires: knowledge of letter values and divine correspondences, understanding of cosmic geometry and celestial timing, appropriate mental state, correct materials, proper ritual. In Ibn Turka's framework, talismanic science is not magic compelling spirits but sophisticated technology of imaginal realm. Talismans work because they express cosmic principles; they align practitioner's will with creation's structure. This gives talismanic practice philosophical and theological legitimacy: not sorcery but gnosis applied to practice.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Talismanic science is primary practical expression of lettrism; demonstrates operative efficacy.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court, Ch. 4.

concepts.name: Peripatetic Philosophy
concepts.literal_meaning: Philosophy of those who walk (Aristotelian school)
concepts.card: **Al-Falsafa al-Mashaʾiya** (Peripatetic Philosophy). The Aristotelian philosophical tradition as transmitted and developed in Islamic world. Emphasizes rational inquiry, logical syllogism, study of natural world, metaphysics grounded in being and causation. Ibn Turka synthesized peripatetic logic and metaphysics with [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], arguing that occult science achieves what peripatetic philosophy merely attempts—systematic knowledge of causation and being.
concepts.body: **Peripatetic philosophy** (*al-falsafa al-mashaʾiya*) refers to the Aristotelian tradition as developed and transmitted in the Islamic world. The name derives from Aristotle's practice of teaching while walking (*peripateo*) in the Lyceum. Islamic philosophers—al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina—adopted and adapted Aristotelian logic, metaphysics, and natural philosophy, integrating them with Islamic theology and the philosophical heritage of Greek Neoplatonism. Key commitments: (1) Reason (*ʿaql*) is primary tool for understanding reality. (2) Logic (syllogistic reasoning) provides rigorous methodology. (3) Being (*wujud*) is fundamental category; understanding causation requires understanding gradations and dependencies of being. (4) Metaphysics is possible: systematic knowledge of principles transcending particular things. By Ibn Turka's era, peripatetic philosophy was the dominant intellectual framework across Islamic world. But Ibn Turka and his circle saw its limitations: peripatetic method, while rigorous, remained abstract and speculative. It described cosmic structure but did not engage it operatively. Peripatetic philosophers asked *how* creation unfolds; Ibn Turka asked *how to participate in its unfolding*. By integrating peripatetic logic with [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], Ibn Turka claimed to achieve what peripatetic philosophy merely attempted—systematic, rationally grounded knowledge of causation and being that is simultaneously operative (producing real effects). In this sense, Ibn Turka's system transcends peripatetic philosophy by incorporating and surpassing it.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Peripatetic philosophy is the dominant rational framework Ibn Turka synthesizes with and transcends through lettrism.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Powers of One, pp. 100-140.

concepts.name: Sufism
concepts.card: **Al-Tasawwuf** (Sufism). Islamic mysticism emphasizing direct experiential knowledge of the divine through discipline, contemplation, and often ecstatic experience. Developed systematically from 9th century onward; by Ibn Turka's era, Sufism was integral to Islamic orthodoxy. [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi]], [[suhrawardi|Suhrawardi]], [[al-ghazali|Al-Ghazali]], and other philosophical predecessors were Sufi-philosophers. Ibn Turka inherited and operationalized Sufi gnosis through lettrism, positioning occult science as Sufi practice systematized into rational discipline.
concepts.body:
## Sufism: Islamic Mysticism and Spiritual Practice

**Al-Tasawwuf** (Sufism) is Islamic mysticism—the disciplined pursuit of direct experiential knowledge (*dhawq*; literally "tasting") of divine reality. Sufism emerged in the 8th-9th centuries as ascetic movement emphasizing renunciation, devotion, and intimate knowledge of God. By the medieval period, it had become systematized into orders (*tariqas*) with formal training, ritual practices, and hierarchical initiation. Key Sufi commitments: (1) Reason alone cannot reach ultimate truth; direct mystical intuition is necessary. (2) The soul possesses faculties beyond intellect—faculties for perceiving divine light and truth. (3) Ascetic discipline, remembrance (*dhikr*), and sincere devotion purify the soul and grant illumination. (4) The spiritual master (*shaykh*) guides disciples on the path. By Ibn Turka's era, Sufism was thoroughly integrated into Islamic orthodoxy. Major philosophical-theologians—[[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi]], [[suhrawardi|Suhrawardi]], [[al-ghazali|Al-Ghazali]]—were simultaneously Sufi mystics and systematic philosophers. Sufism provided the conceptual vocabulary and experiential framework for occult philosophy: if the soul can experience divine light directly, if mystical knowledge is genuine, then the soul's interaction with the imaginal realm and its deployment of lettrist gnosis are not irrational but expressions of mystical capacity. Ibn Turka inherited Sufi gnosis and transformed it: where Sufi masters cultivated mystical states through meditation and discipline, Ibn Turka systematized the underlying principles and made them operative through lettrist-talismanic technique. Sufi mysticism became Sufi science.

## Experience as evidence

The Sufi claim that matters most for Ibn Turka's project is epistemological rather than devotional: that direct experiential knowledge — *dhawq*, tasting — is **knowledge**, not feeling. [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]] had established that much for the mainstream, and once it is granted, the soul's perception of the [[imaginal-realm|imaginal realm]] counts as evidence rather than as reverie.

Ibn Turka takes the concession and does something with it the Sufi tradition largely had not. Where a Sufi master cultivated states through discipline and remembrance, he systematised the principles those states disclose and made them operative through [[ilm-al-huruf|letters]]. Contemplation becomes computation. That is also, precisely, the move his critics objected to — and it is why his relations with organised Sufism were as awkward as [[qasim-i-anvar|his letters]] show them to be: he kept the company of Sufis while criticising the institution in print.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Sufism is the experiential-spiritual foundation upon which Ibn Turka builds his rational occult science; all mystical vocabulary derives from Sufi tradition.
literature: Chittick, William C. The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination.

concepts.name: Occult Science as Universal System
concepts.card: **Occult Science as Universal System**. The core historiographical claim that Ibn Turka and the Isfahan Circle systematized Islamic lettrism, talismanism, and numerology into a comprehensive philosophy claiming universal validity—a science encompassing metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, cosmology, and operative practice. Not marginal superstition but legitimate intellectual achievement rivaling any philosophical school. Melvin-Koushki's central argument.
concepts.body:
The claim that Islamic occultism constitutes a genuine universal science—this is the animating thesis of Melvin-Koushki's entire body of work and the central historiographical claim of Ibn Turka's own project. What did occultism offer that rational philosophy did not? (1) Integration of knowledge and practice: peripatetic philosophy described the cosmos; occult science engaged it operatively. (2) Rigor grounded in systematic principle: not folk magic or superstition but coherent system derived from fundamental doctrines (divine names, letters, Pythagorean numbers). (3) Universality: not provincial tradition but claim to encompass all knowledge—metaphysics via cosmology, epistemology via gnosis, ethics via attunement to cosmic principles. (4) Legitimacy within orthodoxy: by grounding lettrist science in Ibn Arabi's metaphysics and Pythagorean philosophy, Ibn Turka positioned it not as heresy but as sophisticated development within Islamic orthodoxy. The claim to universality is not arrogance but serious metaphysical commitment: if letters are cosmic principles and divine names are ontological foundations, then knowledge of letters and names is knowledge of reality itself—hence universal. This positioning of occult science as universal system represents a major historiographical revaluation: instead of viewing Islamic philosophy as decline into mysticism and formalism, we see a tradition of genuine innovation and intellectual achievement.

## What 'universal' is actually claiming

The word is doing precise work and is worth unpacking, because it is the claim on which everything else rests.

A science is universal, in Ibn Turka's sense, if its object is the principle by which all things are constituted. His argument is that letters and [[divine-names|divine names]] are exactly that: creation unfolds through them, so knowledge of them is knowledge of creation as such, and not of one region of it. This is why he is not content to place [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] among the sciences — a science of everything cannot be one item in a list.

The claim is also what distinguishes his project from what preceded it. Occult practice before him could be defended as *useful*, or as *permitted*, or as *inherited*. Ibn Turka defends it as **systematic**: derived from stated principles, answerable to [[pythagorean-cosmology|mathematics]], and therefore assessable as true or false rather than merely effective or ineffective. That is the difference between a body of technique and a philosophy, and it is the difference he spent the *Mafāḥiṣ* establishing.

It should be said plainly that the claim is very strong and was not conceded. The [[neoplatonism|anti-occultist coalition]] — Ibn Sīnā, [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]], Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Khaldūn — denied that these were sciences at all, and Ibn Turka's move into the mathematical sciences is an answer to them rather than a victory over them.
concepts.hierarchy_note: This historiographical frame unites all entries; it is the meta-argument justifying the entire project.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography.

concepts.name: Neoplatonism
concepts.card: **Neoplatonism**. The late-antique emanationist philosophy of Plotinus and Proclus, which reached Islamdom in Arabic translation and was never, in Melvin-Koushki's usage, quite separable from its Pythagorean twin — he writes of *neopythagorean-neoplatonic* philosophy as one tradition. Ibn Turka's contribution was not to receive it but to **reclassify** it: he treated this philosophy as prophetically revealed rather than merely Greek, and made its mathematics the ground on which the occult sciences could be defended as sciences at all.
concepts.body:
## Neoplatonism, and what Ibn Turka did to it

**The tradition.** Neoplatonism — the emanationist system of Plotinus (d. 270), systematised by Porphyry and Proclus — holds that reality flows from a transcendent One through descending grades of being, and that the soul ascends by retracing that descent. It entered Arabic through the translation movement, generally fused with Pythagorean number-metaphysics. Melvin-Koushki treats the pair as a single tradition throughout, writing of **neopythagorean-neoplatonic philosophy** rather than of two separable schools (*Powers of One*, 127–28).

**The problem it was made to solve.** By Ibn Turka's lifetime the occult sciences — *al-ʿulūm al-gharība*, the 'strange sciences' — had absorbed four centuries of hostile polemic from a formidable coalition. Melvin-Koushki notes that anti-occultism is one of the few subjects on which philosophers like Ibn Sīnā, theologians like Ghazālī, traditionalists like Ibn Taymiyya and historians like Ibn Khaldūn find common cause, joined by al-Ashʿarī, Fārābī, al-Bāqillānī and Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār (*Powers of One*, 1). The charge was that these were not sciences.

**Ibn Turka's contribution.** The Persianate answer, of which he is the central theoretician, was to **move the occult sciences out of the natural sciences and into the mathematical sciences** — a reclassification that reasserted their legitimacy on ground the polemicists could not easily contest (*Powers of One*, 1). Melvin-Koushki names the threefold process **mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and sanctification**, and locates it in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran. Neoplatonism is the metaphysics that makes the move coherent: if being descends by graded emanation, and number governs the descent, then a science of number and letter is a science of causation itself.

**The move that was genuinely his.** Ibn Turka did not present this philosophy as a Greek inheritance. He identified its greatest exponents — the Imams and the ancients, with their disciples in every age — with the quranic phrase *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār*, 'those possessed of hands and vision': the coterie of inspired thinkers who preserved **prophetically revealed** neopythagorean-neoplatonic philosophy in written form. The philosophy is therefore not borrowed but recovered, and its authority revelatory rather than merely rational. The phrase appears to have entered common usage as a designation for sages and philosophers generally from Ibn Turka onward (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

**What changed.** The consequences ran well past his death. Melvin-Koushki argues that this mathematicalization is the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context both for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy by the Samarkand Observatory in the 9th/15th century and for the resurgence of neoplatonic-neopythagorean philosophy in Safavid Iran in the 10th/16th and 11th/17th — in the course of which **Ibn Sīnā himself, the tradition's most formidable anti-occultist, was posthumously transformed into a neopythagorean-occultist** (*Powers of One*, 1). These processes, he notes, have previously been studied in atomistic isolation.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: The Mathematicalization of the Occult Sciences in the High Persianate Tradition*, 1, 127–28.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66.

concepts.name: Timurid Court Patronage
concepts.card: The institutional and political context enabling Ibn Turka and Isfahan Circle. Timurid rulers patronized scholars, established courts as intellectual centers, created conditions for systematic philosophical innovation.
concepts.body: Timurid dynasty (1370–1506) under figures like Shahrukh actively patronized scholars and artists. Courts in Samarkand, Isfahan, Yazd became magnets for intellectuals. This patronage enabled Ibn Turka's work and the Isfahan Circle's activities.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.

concepts.name: Mamluk Cairo Context
concepts.card: Cairo was the intellectual and political center of the Mamluk Sultanate (1250–1517). Akhlati and other Ibn Turka's predecessors worked in Cairo courts. Mamluk patronage of scholars influenced Timurid court structures.
concepts.body: Mamluk Cairo was the largest Muslim city and intellectual center. It provided patronage for scholars including Akhlati. The Mamluk court model influenced how Timurid courts operated.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.

concepts.name: Walāya
concepts.literal_meaning: Sainthood; sanctity; proximity to God; the authority of the friend of God
concepts.card: **Walāya** — sainthood, or the authority that comes of proximity to God. The most consequential reclassification in Melvin-Koushki's account, and the one usually missed: alongside their move into the mathematical sciences, the occult sciences were recast as **sciences of walāya**. This, he argues, is what *alone* explains the surge in patronage of professional occultists at the Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts in the runup to the Islamic millennium (1592 CE). A science of walāya is not a technique anyone may practise; it is the prerogative of the sanctified.
concepts.body:
## Walāya: occultism as a science of sanctity

**The term.** *Walāya* denotes sainthood, sanctity, and the proximity to God from which spiritual authority derives; a *walī* is a friend of God. In Shiʿi usage it carries the further charge of the Imams' authority. This is not peripheral vocabulary: it recurs across every major source in the corpus, some two hundred times in total.

**The reclassification.** Melvin-Koushki's thesis has two limbs, and walāya is the one usually overlooked. The occult sciences were shifted from the natural to the [[neoplatonism|mathematical]] sciences to reassert their scientific legitimacy; they were **simultaneously reclassified as the sciences of walāya**. He is emphatic about the explanatory weight the second move carries — it *alone*, he writes, explains the massive increase in patronage of professional occultists at the Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts in the runup to the Islamic millennium of 1592 CE (*Powers of One*, 1).

**Why the second limb matters.** Mathematicalization answers the epistemological objection: is this a science? Sanctification answers a different and, at court, more urgent question: who may practise it, and why should a ruler pay for them? A science of walāya cannot be picked up by anyone with a manual. It belongs to those near to God — which makes the occultist not a technician but a figure of religious authority, and his patronage a matter of dynastic legitimacy rather than curiosity. This is the mechanism underneath the [[isfahan-circle|occult court]].

**The Shiʿi thread.** The lineage runs through the Imams. Ibn Turka reports that the holy Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq greatly vaunted the science of letters, and that 'those who cleave to the threshold of his walāya have penned numerous works on the subject' (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66). Walāya is thus at once the ground of the science's authority and the channel of its transmission — the reason a chain of lettrist writing exists at all.

**Bearing on Ibn Turka.** It positions him. He is not merely systematising a technique; he is claiming for [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] the standing of a sanctified science, whose exponents are the *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār* — the Imams, the ancients and their disciples in every age — who preserved prophetically revealed philosophy in written form. It also explains how the science travelled after him: what reached the Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts was not a body of techniques but a claim about who stands close to God.

## Why "sanctification" is the second half of a two-part thesis

It is easy to read Melvin-Koushki as arguing one thing — that the occult sciences were
mathematicalized — and to treat walāya as a footnote. The text does not permit that. The
formulation is deliberately double: the occult sciences **were gradually but definitively
shifted from the natural to the mathematical sciences** as a means of reasserting their
scientific legitimacy, and **they were simultaneously reclassified as the sciences of
walāya** (*Powers of One*, 1).

The two moves answer different objections from different audiences.

**Mathematicalization answers the philosophers.** Against Ibn Sīnā, Ghazālī, Ibn Taymiyya
and Ibn Khaldūn, who denied that these were sciences at all, the reply is that they belong
among the mathematical disciplines, whose credentials were not in dispute.

**Sanctification answers the court.** A ruler does not need to be told that a discipline is
epistemically respectable; he needs to know who may practise it and why he should pay them.
A science of walāya is not available to anyone with a manual. It belongs to those near to
God, which makes the practitioner a figure of religious authority and his retention a matter
of dynastic legitimacy.

Melvin-Koushki gives the second limb the heavier causal load, and says so: it is this that
**alone explains the massive increase in patronage of professional occultists at the
Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts in the runup to the Islamic millennium** of 1592
(*Powers of One*, 1). Not mathematics — sanctity — is what opened the treasuries.

## The Imams as the channel

The lineage runs through the Imams, which is what ties walāya to
[[imamophilism|imamophilism]] rather than to formal Shiʿism. Ibn Turka reports that the
**holy Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq greatly vaunted this science, and those who cleave to the
threshold of his walāya have penned numerous works on the subject** (*Of Islamic
Grammatology*, 66).

The phrasing is worth attention. Authorship is attributed not to a school or a lineage of
teachers but to *those who cleave to the threshold of his walāya* — proximity to sanctity
is what qualifies a person to write on letters at all. Walāya is simultaneously the ground
of the science's authority and the channel of its transmission.

## Timing: why the millennium matters

The surge in patronage is dated to the runup to the Islamic millennium of 1592, and the
dating is not incidental. A court approaching a millennial turn has an acute interest in
knowing where it stands in sacred history and in employing people who can say. A science of
walāya supplies both a reading of the times and a sanctified reader. This is the mechanism
underneath the [[isfahan-circle|occult court]], and it explains why the phenomenon is
transregional — Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts arriving at the same solution because
they faced the same calendar.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka used the term with the same technical force** the later tradition
  gives it is not laid out in the sources in hand.
- **How the reclassification was argued** — the specific texts in which occult sciences are
  formally reassigned to walāya — is treated by Melvin-Koushki at the level of the movement
  rather than the individual treatise.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Walāya is the second limb of Melvin-Koushki's thesis, paired with mathematicalization; together they explain the legitimacy and the patronage of the occult sciences.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.

concepts.name: Ḥurūfism
concepts.card: **Ḥurūfism** — the messianic letter-movement founded by Fażl Allāh Astarābādī (d. 796/1394), which read the letters as announcing a new dispensation. It is the heresy Ibn Turka had to be distinguished from, and the charge on which he was exiled from Herat in 1427. The distinction is not technique but **motive**: the Ḥurūfīs proclaimed a new revelation; the lettrists claimed to be working *within* the tradition to extend human knowledge.
concepts.body:
## Ḥurūfism, and the line Ibn Turka had to draw

**The movement.** Fażl Allāh Astarābādī (d. 796/1394) taught that the letters disclose a new phase of revelation, and his followers — the Ḥurūfiyya — carried that claim into open messianism across Iran and Anatolia. Both they and Ibn Turka worked on letters. That shared subject matter is precisely the problem.

**The distinction is motive, not method.** Melvin-Koushki puts the difference plainly: what separates the lettrists from the Ḥurūfīs and the other messianic movements of early 9th/15th-century Iran is motive — *the gnostic Hurufis proclaim a new, Persian dispensation; the messianic Sufis promote themselves as political saviors; the lettrists present themselves as occult philosophers working within the tradition to expand the boundaries of human knowledge* (*The Quest*, 456).

Ibn Turka is himself, by any standard, a profoundly millenarian thinker: he proclaims the advent of a new age, heralded by heavenly portent, in which the occult knowledge of the Imams and the ancients will be made manifest. What keeps this inside orthodoxy is its insistence on **the binding finality of the dispensation given through Muḥammad** (*The Quest*, 456). A new age of knowledge, not a new prophecy. The whole of his position rests on that distinction, and it is a fine one.

**Why the charge stuck to him.** Because it was not baseless. Fażl Allāh arrived in Isfahan around 766/1365 and quickly became famous as a dream interpreter, and Ḥurūfī sources record that **Ibn Turka's own father Afżal al-Dīn and his elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] sought him out there to have their dreams interpreted**. Naṣr Allāh Nāfajī's *Khwābnāma* preserves the episode (*The Quest*, ch. 1, and Eichner, 'Afḍal al-Dīn Turka', EI3).

Melvin-Koushki is careful about what this does and does not show: the contact does not imply Ḥurūfī inclinations on the part of the two Turkas, and the hagiographical point of the story is to establish Fażl Allāh's fame as a Sufi *before* his messianic transformation — respected scholars of the religious sciences came to him for counsel. But a family documented as having consulted the founder of the Ḥurūfiyya gives a prosecutor something to work with, and in 1427 a prosecutor used it.

**The cost.** [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]] court exiled Ibn Turka from Herat alongside [[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], the official excuse being a putative Ḥurūfī connection (*The Quest*, 456 n.16). The science and the heresy were close enough in appearance that the difference had to be argued, and arguing it was a lifetime's work.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Ḥurūfism is the boundary case for [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]: same material, different claim, and the distinction is what Ibn Turka spent his career defending.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 456 and ch. 1.
Eichner, Heidrun. 'Afḍal al-Dīn Turka.' *Encyclopaedia of Islam*, THREE.

concepts.name: Shiʿi-Sunnism (imamophilism)
concepts.literal_meaning: Devotion to the Imams without formal Shiʿi affiliation
concepts.card: **Shiʿi-Sunnism**, or **imamophilism** — reverence for the Imams held without a formal Shiʿi confessional commitment. Melvin-Koushki calls it a **defining feature of 9th/15th-century Islamic religiosity**, particularly in Iran and particularly in esotericist circles, and it is his answer to the long argument about whether Ibn Turka was 'really' a Shiʿi or a Sunni. The question is anachronistic; the position is the period's own.
concepts.body:
## Neither, and deliberately

**The problem it solves.** Ibn Turka's confessional identity has been read both ways. Henry Corbin embraced him as a standard-issue Shiʿi esotericist; Leonard Lewisohn, reading the [[nafsat-al-masdur|apologies]], presents him as an orthodox Sunni Sufi thinker. Melvin-Koushki rejects both: Ibn Turka's ambiguous confessional position is best described as **Shiʿi-Sunnism or imamophilism** (*The Quest*, 7).

**Why it is not fence-sitting.** The category is not a compromise between two real options but a description of what was normal. Deep reverence for the Imams as sources of esoteric knowledge, held without the juridical and political commitments of Twelver Shiʿism, was a defining feature of fifteenth-century Islamic religiosity — most of all in Iran, and most of all among esotericists. Reading the period through the hardened Safavid confessional boundary that came *after* it produces a question the sources are not answering.

**How it shows up in the work.** Ibn Turka identifies the greatest exponents of the perennial philosophy as the Imams and the ancients together with their disciples in every age, the *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār*. He reports that Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq greatly vaunted the science of letters and that those who cleave to the threshold of his [[walaya|walāya]] have written much on it. The Imams function as guarantors of **knowledge**, which is a different office from the one Twelver jurisprudence assigns them.

**The historiographical payoff.** Insisting on the label 'Shiʿi' or 'Sunni' for Ibn Turka does not sharpen the picture, it flattens it — and, as with the [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd*]], the flattening has consequences: a man sorted into a confessional box is easy to file as a mystical philosopher and hard to see as an [[occult-science-universal|occult philosopher]] with a systematic programme.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Imamophilism is the confessional setting of the whole project; it explains why the Imams appear as authorities on lettrism without the entry being a Shiʿi one.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 6–7.

bibliography.author: Matthew Melvin-Koushki
bibliography.title: The Quest for a Universal Science: The Occult Philosophy of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432) and Intellectual Millenarianism in Early Timurid Iran
bibliography.card: Matthew Melvin-Koushki's Yale dissertation is the foundational modern treatment of Ibn Turka's life, thought, and historical significance. Based on direct engagement with Ibn Turka's manuscripts and the vast corpus of Melvin-Koushki's own scholarship on Islamic occultism, this 615-page work establishes Ibn Turka as a central figure in late medieval intellectual history. The dissertation situates Ibn Turka within the transregional network of the "New Brethren of Purity" and demonstrates that his lettrist philosophy was not marginal esotericism but a sophisticated universal science grounded in Pythagorean principles and integrated with the best scholarship of his era.
bibliography.body:
## Matthew Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale, 2012)

Matthew Melvin-Koushki's 2012 Yale dissertation remains the authoritative monographic treatment of Ibn Turka and marks a watershed in Islamic intellectual history. Before this work, Ibn Turka was known primarily to specialists in Islamic philosophy and mysticism, often dismissed as a minor figure or interesting curiosity. Melvin-Koushki's dissertation transformed scholarly understanding by demonstrating that Ibn Turka was in fact a central architect of a vast intellectual network and a theorist of occult philosophy whose ambitions rivaled those of contemporary European thinkers (Pico della Mirandola, John Dee, Giordano Bruno).

### Argument and Method

The dissertation's central claim is that Ibn Turka's occult philosophy—specifically his systematization of Islamic lettrism (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*)—represents not a deviation from rational philosophy but rather an alternative universal science grounded in Pythagorean-Neoplatonic principles. Where previous scholarship treated lettrism as mystical or marginal, Melvin-Koushki demonstrates that Ibn Turka approached it rigorously, integrating it with formal logic, metaphysics, and natural philosophy.

Melvin-Koushki's method is archival and textual. He works from Ibn Turka's surviving manuscripts—including the unpublished *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries), *Risālat al-Barzakh* (Treatise on the Isthmus), and dozens of shorter treatises—reading them with precision and integrating them with contemporary sources and modern scholarship. He also contextualizes Ibn Turka within the broader network of late medieval occultists, showing how Cairo (under Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī), Isfahan (under Ibn Turka), and other centers were connected through overlapping circles of scholars and patrons.

### Key Contributions

**1. Excavation of the New Brethren Network.** Melvin-Koushki demonstrates that Ibn Turka was part of a self-conscious intellectual network calling itself the "New Brethren of Purity" (*Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ al-jadīd*), deliberately invoking the medieval Brethren and their encyclopedic project. This network stretched from Cairo through Anatolia to Iran, Central Asia, and India, united by a common commitment to retrieving, systematizing, and applying the occult sciences for the advancement of humanity and the power of empire.

**2. Demonstration of Philosophical Rigor.** Against orientalist dismissals of Islamic occultism as superstition, Melvin-Koushki shows Ibn Turka engaging with the full apparatus of Islamic peripatetic philosophy, Neoplatonic metaphysics, and formal logic. His lettrist treatises are philosophically rigorous, technically sophisticated, and integrated with mainstream scholarship.

**3. Pythagorean Framing.** Melvin-Koushki argues that Ibn Turka's central innovation was grounding lettrism explicitly in Pythagorean mathematics and cosmology. By demonstrating that the Arabic alphabet and divine names encode numerical relationships reflecting cosmic principles, Ibn Turka gave lettrism mathematical legitimacy and scope unmatched by previous treatments.

**4. Imperial Significance.** The dissertation shows that Ibn Turka's occult philosophy was not an academic abstraction but a tool for imperial power. His synthesis of lettrism, alchemy, talismanic magic, and astrology was designed to serve Timurid rulers, enabling them to understand and transform reality at every scale—from personal psychology to cosmic history.

### Structure and Content

The dissertation is organized into two major parts:

**Part 1: Analysis and Contextualization.** This section presents Ibn Turka's biography, places him within the Akhlāṭī network, analyzes the development of Islamic lettrism from Ibn ʿArabī through Ibn Turka, and explores how his philosophy integrates peripatetic-illuminationist reasoning with Sufi mysticism. Chapters examine his theory of the cosmos, his doctrine of divine names and letters, his political philosophy, and his vision of human perfection (*al-insān al-kāmil*).

**Part 2: Editions and Translations.** The second part provides edited texts and full English translations of five of Ibn Turka's most important minor lettrist treatises, making them accessible to English-speaking scholars for the first time.

### Impact and Reception

Since publication, the dissertation has become the foundation for all subsequent work on Ibn Turka and Islamic occultism. Melvin-Koushki's subsequent publications (over 40 articles and books since 2012) have expanded on the dissertation's arguments, exploring specific aspects of Ibn Turka's thought (Pythagorean cosmology, talismanic magic, grammatology, empire and occultism, etc.) and situating him within broader narratives of early modern intellectual history.

The dissertation has also influenced how scholars understand the early modern period globally. By placing an Islamic occultist at the center of early modern thought, Melvin-Koushki challenges Eurocentric narratives that see occult philosophy as a European phenomenon. Ibn Turka's work on magical-mathematical empire provides a non-European parallel (and arguably a more sophisticated treatment) to Pico, Dee, and Bruno.

### Critical Reception

The dissertation has been widely praised for its originality, rigor, and scope. It has also proven controversial in some quarters—scholars invested in sharp divisions between "science" and "superstition," or in Islamic intellectual history defined narrowly by theology and jurisprudence, have sometimes resisted Melvin-Koushki's elevation of occultism to central importance. Yet the weight of evidence and the sophistication of Melvin-Koushki's argument have gradually shifted the consensus.

sections.heading: Abstract and thesis
sections.summary: States the problem the whole work exists to correct. Ibn Turka is the foremost occult philosopher of Timurid Iran, yet **half his oeuvre remains in manuscript — including, predictably, the lettrist works**, assumed to be the most marginal part of his thought. The irony is named precisely: it is exactly *because* he has been acclaimed since the nineteenth century as the synthesizer linking Ibn ʿArabī to Mullā Ṣadrā that he was marginalised, since such acclaim obscures the occultist tenor of the larger project, abstracts it from its historical context and robs it of its animating virtue. The stated burden of the study is to present and contextualise the central lettrist component on the basis of the unpublished works, with particular attention to the *K. al-Mafāḥiṣ*, 'a summa of intellectual lettrism'.

sections.heading: Chapter 1 — Biography and religio-historical context
sections.summary: The life and the world it happened in. Establishes the Isfahani scholarly family, the education under his elder brother Ṣadr al-Dīn for twenty-five years alongside Qāḍīzāda Rūmī, the fifteen years abroad under Akhlāṭī in Cairo, and the confessional setting — which the chapter argues is best called Shiʿi-Sunnism or imamophilism rather than forced into either box. Also handles the Ḥurūfī question, including the awkward fact that Ibn Turka's own father and brother had consulted Fażl Allāh Astarābādī in Isfahan.

sections.heading: Chapter 2 — Annotated list of works
sections.summary: The bibliographical foundation. **25 Persian and 19 (or 20) Arabic works — 44 or 45 in total — plus a small dīvān, one ijāza, and 58 letters, fragments and notes**; twenty-two have been edited or printed in some form. Each work is briefly summarised and all known manuscript copies listed. The list builds on Akram Jūdī-Niʿmatī's, supplemented and corrected. Dating rests wherever possible on the colophons of MS Majlis 10196, with an explicit caution that in many cases composition and transcription cannot be told apart.

sections.heading: Chapter 3 — The universalist lettrist project
sections.summary: The core argument. §3.1 traces the popularisation of lettrism as a universal science from Ibn Turka's return to Iran c. 810/1408: the courts of the Timurid princes of western Iran proved a receptive audience, first Pīr-Muḥammad at Shiraz and then Iskandar Sulṭān at Isfahan. Iskandar — known for his imamophilism and esotericist bent, and accounted the leading Timurid patron of culture in the early Shahrukhid period — may personally have commissioned the *R. Ḥurūf*, and was presumably responsible for installing Ibn Turka in the **hereditary** judgeship of Isfahan.

sections.heading: Chapters 4–6 — Lettrism against philosophy and Sufism
sections.summary: The project set against its two nearest rivals: peripatetic-illuminationist philosophy on one side and Sufism on the other. The running theme is an invidious comparison in which lettrism wins on scope — the faux-universal concepts of philosophical speculation notwithstanding, **only the letter encompasses all that is and is not, all that can and cannot be**; it alone is the *coincidentia oppositorum*, and hence lettrism is the only truly universal science.

sections.heading: Chapter 7 — Translations from the Book of Inquiries
sections.summary: Largely translated sections from the *K. al-Mafāḥiṣ*, giving the reader the summa in Ibn Turka's own words rather than in paraphrase — including the fourfold treatment of the letters according to their numerological (*iḥṣāʾī*), symbological (*kitābī*) and phonological (*kalāmī*) forms, and as they are in themselves (*fī anfusi-hā*).

sections.heading: Part 2 — Editions and translations
sections.summary: Editions and/or translations of five of the minor lettrist treatises: the primary-source apparatus that makes the argument of Part 1 checkable.

sections.heading: Addenda — Chronology, 33–36
sections.summary: A dated chronology of the life and works, from the birth to the death at Herat in 835/1432. Ibn Turka's own events unitalicized, other events italicized, the lettrist works bolded. Melvin-Koushki flags that given the sparseness of the record some dates are conjectured or approximate; most rest on the colophons of MS Majlis 10196 and the two collections of letters, with select political events from Manz, *Power, Politics and Religion*. **This is the source of the portal's own chronology page.**

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: Powers of One: The Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context
bibliography.card: **Matthew Melvin-Koushki, Powers of One** (BRILL, 2017, 74 pp). Focused study of Ibn Turka's synthesis of Pythagorean mathematics with Islamic lettrism. Argues that Ibn Turka's explicit grounding of lettrism in Pythagorean cosmology represents a revolutionary moment in Islamic intellectual history—positioning occult science as universal system rivaling any philosophical school. Essential for understanding Ibn Turka's mathematical framework.
bibliography.body: **Matthew Melvin-Koushki, Powers of One: The Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context** (Boston: BRILL, 2017, 74 pages). A tightly argued monograph extracted from Melvin-Koushki's larger body of work, focusing specifically on Ibn Turka's adoption and deployment of Pythagorean philosophy. Melvin-Koushki establishes: (1) Pythagorean ideas reached Islamic world through Neoplatonic transmission, Greek texts preserved in Arabic translation, and Byzantine scholarly contact. (2) Earlier Islamic philosophers (al-Kindi, al-Farabi) engaged Pythagoreanism but did not fully synthesize it with Islamic occultism. (3) Ibn Turka was the first to explicitly declare that Islamic lettrism is fundamentally Pythagorean—that letters and their numerical values encode cosmic ratios and mathematical principles governing creation. (4) This move was revolutionary: it gave lettrism mathematical legitimacy, connected it to ancient philosophy (lending historical pedigree), and positioned it as universal science encompassing reason, mysticism, and practice. Powers of One is essential reading for understanding Ibn Turka's intellectual project and the claim that occult philosophy represents genuine scientific advancement, not remnant superstition.

sections.heading: The thesis, p. 1
sections.summary: The densest page in the corpus. Certain occult sciences — astrology, lettrism and geomancy — were gradually but definitively **shifted from the natural to the mathematical sciences** as a means of reasserting their scientific legitimacy in the face of four centuries of anti-occultist polemic running from Ibn Sīnā to Ibn Khaldūn. They were **simultaneously reclassified as the sciences of walāya**, which alone explains the massive increase in patronage of professional occultists at the Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts in the runup to the Islamic millennium of 1592.

sections.heading: The consequence for the history of science
sections.summary: The mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and sanctification of occultism in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran is argued to be the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context both for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy at the Samarkand Observatory and for the resurgence of neoplatonic-neopythagorean philosophy in Safavid Iran — in the course of which Ibn Sīnā himself was transformed into a neopythagorean-occultist. These processes, he notes, have heretofore been studied in atomistic isolation.

sections.heading: The anti-occultist coalition
sections.summary: Names the opposition precisely, and it is formidable: anti-occultism is one of the few subjects on which philosophers like Ibn Sīnā, theologians like Ghazālī, traditionalists like Ibn Taymiyya and historians like Ibn Khaldūn find common cause, joined by al-Ashʿarī, Fārābī, al-Bāqillānī and Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār. The *ʿulūm al-gharība* had been a site of scholarly controversy since they entered Islamdom in the 2nd/8th century.

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: Of Islamic Grammatology: Towards a Philosophy of the Arabic Letter
bibliography.card: **Matthew Melvin-Koushki, Of Islamic Grammatology** (BRILL, 2016, 73 pp). Explores how Islamic lettrism positions the Arabic letter as fundamental ontological and epistemological principle. Traces development from early Islamic exegesis through Ibn Arabi to Ibn Turka. Central for understanding letters as not merely symbols but cosmic entities encoding divine principles.
bibliography.body: **Matthew Melvin-Koushki, Of Islamic Grammatology: Towards a Philosophy of the Arabic Letter** (Boston: BRILL, 2016, 73 pages). Grammatology—the study of writing systems as philosophical and cosmological frameworks—becomes Islamic when the letter itself is understood as cosmic principle. Melvin-Koushki traces this development: from Qur'anic exegesis that saw letters as carriers of divine meaning, through Ibn Arabi's theory of names and letters, to Ibn Turka's full systematization of lettrism. The book establishes that Islamic lettrism is not superstition but a sophisticated epistemology: it claims that letters are the fundamental units through which knowledge and reality alike are constituted. Mastery of letters grants mastery of meaning, causation, and cosmic structure. Essential for understanding the theoretical foundations of Ibn Turka's entire project.
bibliography.access_note: Published monograph; available through university libraries and BRILL

sections.heading: The letter as ontological principle
sections.summary: Grammatology — the study of writing as a philosophical framework — becomes Islamic when the letter is itself a cosmic principle. Traces the development from Qur'anic exegesis through Ibn ʿArabī to Ibn Turka's full systematisation.

sections.heading: The Book of Inquiries, p. 66
sections.summary: Dates and places the summa: begun shortly after *Of Letters* and again almost certainly at the instance of Iskandar Sulṭān, **completed 823/1420 and revised and expanded 828/1425**; 'the first Arabic summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism'. Sets out the fourfold schema of the letter. Notes that lettrist theory is necessarily predicated on the **uncreatedness of the Qur'an**, and that Ibn Turka censures Zamakhsharī's *Kashshāf* for failing to recognise the intrinsic ontological majesty of the quranic letters.

sections.heading: The perennial philosophers
sections.summary: Ibn Turka identifies the greatest exponents of the perennial philosophy — the Imams and the ancients with their disciples in every age — with the quranic *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār*, those possessed of hands and vision, who preserved prophetically revealed neopythagorean-neoplatonic philosophy in written form. The phrase appears to enter general usage for sages and philosophers from Ibn Turka onward.

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: The Occult Court: Magic, Medicine, and Mathematics in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth-Century Isfahan
bibliography.card: **Matthew Melvin-Koushki, The Occult Court** (BRILL, 2025). Latest major work; contextualizes Ibn Turka within Timurid court politics, medical practice, and imperial administration. Demonstrates that occult science was not marginal to political power but central: talismanic knowledge, astrological timing, and lettrist consultation shaped statecraft. Essential for understanding Isfahan Circle as institutional nexus.
bibliography.body: Melvin-Koushki's newest monograph contextualizes Ibn Turka and the Isfahan Circle within the actual political and administrative structures of the Timurid court. The thesis: occult science was not a marginal pursuit of eccentric scholars but a sophisticated technology of imperial governance. Talismans were created to protect princes, ensure fertility, secure alliances. Astrological timing informed military campaigns. Lettrist consultation shaped policy. By tracing the actual patronage networks, institutional positions, and court roles of Ibn Turka and his circle, Melvin-Koushki shows that occultism was integrated into the machinery of state. This reframes the entire project: Ibn Turka was not an isolated philosopher but a court functionary whose systematization of lettrism served Timurid imperial interests. Essential for understanding Isfahan Circle as operational nexus, not merely intellectual network.
bibliography.access_note: Recently published; available through BRILL and university libraries

sections.heading: Occultism as statecraft
sections.summary: The occult sciences as a technology of imperial governance rather than a marginal pursuit: talismans, astrological timing and lettrist consultation inside the actual machinery of Timurid administration. Reframes Ibn Turka from isolated philosopher to court functionary whose systematisation served imperial interests.

sections.heading: Patronage networks
sections.summary: Traces the concrete patronage relationships, institutional positions and court roles that made the Isfahan Circle an operational nexus rather than merely an intellectual one.

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism and Imaginal Ontology in the Thought of Ibn Turka
bibliography.card: **Matthew Melvin-Koushki, Being with a Capital B** (BRILL, 2023). Examines Ibn Turka's metaphysics: how Pythagorean mathematics and imaginal ontology ground a comprehensive philosophy of being. Shows that Ibn Turka's system is not magic but ontological engineering—restructuring human perception and will to align with cosmic structure. Essential theoretical text.
bibliography.body: Melvin-Koushki's most philosophically ambitious work, examining Ibn Turka's metaphysical foundations. Central argument: Ibn Turka's synthesis of Pythagorean mathematics with imaginal ontology (inherited from Suhrawardi and Ibn Arabi via Qunavi) represents a genuine philosophical achievement—a systematic answer to the question of being and causation. By treating letters as ontological primitives (possessing reality independent of human speech), and by grounding all causation in the imaginal realm where letters and divine names operate, Ibn Turka offers an alternative metaphysics rivaling Aristotelian and Neoplatonic systems. The work positions Ibn Turka not as occultist or mystic alone, but as systematic metaphysician. Essential for understanding that Ibn Turka's project is not irrational superstition but coherent philosophy.

sections.heading: Imaginal ontology
sections.summary: Ibn Turka's metaphysics as a systematic philosophy of being rather than a body of technique: letters as ontological primitives, causation grounded in the imaginal realm, and the whole offered as an alternative to Aristotelian and Neoplatonic systems.

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography: Rethinking Reason, Revelation, and Philosophy in Islamic Thought
bibliography.card: **Melvin-Koushki, Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography** (BRILL, 2020). Methodological framework for understanding Islamic intellectual history not as decline from classical period but as continuous innovation. Positions Ibn Turka and circle as exemplars of genuine philosophical renewal—Islamic Pythagoreanism as alternative intellectual tradition rivaling European Renaissance. Foundational historiographical text.
bibliography.body: Methodological work establishing how to read 14th-15th century Islamic occult philosophy. Melvin-Koushki argues: conventional narratives treat Islamic intellectual history as decline—loss of Greek philosophical legacy, fragmentation into mysticism and formalism. But this framework blinds us to actual innovation. Ibn Turka's synthesis of lettrism and Pythagoreanism is not preservation of earlier thought but creation of new system. Calling it Neopythagorean positions it in comparative context: just as European Renaissance rediscovered and redeployed Platonic philosophy, Islamic occultists rediscovered and redeployed Pythagorean principles—creating Islamic Neopythagoreanism. This historiographical move revalues the entire intellectual tradition and shows that Ibn Turka participates in global philosophical currents, not provincial Islamic scholarship.
bibliography.access_note: Published; available through BRILL and universities

sections.heading: Against the decline thesis
sections.summary: Methodological. Conventional narratives treat post-classical Islamic thought as decline; that frame blinds us to actual innovation. Naming the period's achievement **Neopythagorean** places it in comparative context: as the European Renaissance rediscovered and redeployed Platonic philosophy, Islamic occultists rediscovered and redeployed Pythagorean principles.

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: World as (Arabic) Text: Reading Creation through Letters and Names
bibliography.card: **Melvin-Koushki, World as (Arabic) Text** (BRILL, 2020). Explores how Islamic lettrism positions creation as readable text—cosmos constituted through letters and divine names. Treats cosmology, hermeneutics, and ontology as unified: to read letters is to read creation; mastery of letters grants mastery of being. Philosophical and poetic exploration of lettrist gnosis.
bibliography.body: Philosophical exploration of how Islamic lettrism reconstructs the relationship between language, meaning, and reality. Central claim: creation is text—specifically, Arabic text. The universe unfolds through divine speech; divine names generate reality; letters are cosmic entities. If reality is constituted through letters, then knowledge of letters is knowledge of reality itself. Reading—hermeneutics—becomes ontology. The act of reading the divine text (Qur'an, letters, names) is simultaneous act of reading creation. Ibn Turka's system radicalizes this: by treating letters as operative principles, he shows that reading creation is not passive interpretation but active participation—the reader/practitioner becomes co-creator through understanding and deploying lettrist gnosis. This work connects Qur'anic exegesis, medieval Islamic hermeneutics, and Ibn Turka's occultism into unified vision.
bibliography.access_note: Published; available through BRILL and universities

sections.heading: Creation as text
sections.summary: If reality is constituted through letters, then reading is ontology and hermeneutics is cosmology. Ibn Turka radicalises the position: reading creation is not passive interpretation but active participation.

bibliography.author: Chittick, William C.
bibliography.title: The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination
bibliography.card: **William C. Chittick, The Sufi Path of Knowledge** (SUNY Press, 1989, 410 pp). Comprehensive exposition of Ibn Arabi's metaphysical system, including imaginal realm, divine names, and theophanic knowledge. Essential for understanding conceptual foundations that Ibn Turka inherited and systematized. Though not focused on Ibn Turka, provides crucial theoretical background.
bibliography.body: Chittick's authoritative work on Ibn Arabi provides the clearest exposition of concepts foundational to Ibn Turka's system: the imaginal realm, divine names as principles of manifestation, the macrocosm-microcosm correspondence. Chittick emphasizes that for Ibn Arabi (and subsequently Ibn Turka), mysticism is not irrational or emotional but sophisticated gnosis grounded in rigorous metaphysical principles. His reconstruction of Ibn Arabi's theory of knowledge—how divine truth manifests through imagination, how names function as operative principles—is essential background for understanding Ibn Turka's transformation of these ideas into lettrist science.
bibliography.access_note: Published monograph; widely available in academic libraries

bibliography.author: Corbin, Henry
bibliography.title: History of Islamic Philosophy
bibliography.card: Corbin's magisterial history covering Ibn Arabi, Suhrawardi, and later Islamic philosophy. Essential context for understanding Ibn Turka within broader tradition of Islamic thought.
bibliography.body: Corbin's comprehensive survey situates Ibn Turka within longer historical trajectory of Islamic philosophy. Particularly strong on Illuminationist philosophy and its development through Suhrawardi and Mulla Sadra.

bibliography.author: Nasr, Seyyed Hossein
bibliography.title: Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance
bibliography.card: Nasr argues Islamic sciences were not declinist but generative throughout medieval and early modern periods. Situates occult sciences and Ibn Turka within global intellectual history.
bibliography.body: Positions Islamic philosophy and science as continuous achievement rather than decline. Relevant to understanding Ibn Turka's system as genuine innovation, not preservation.

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: Lettrism, Astrology, and Jazz Philosophy
bibliography.card: Melvin-Koushki's essay on how Ibn Turka's lettrist system constitutes a philosophy of meaning-making comparable to jazz improvisation. Innovative historiographical approach demonstrating ongoing relevance of Ibn Turka's thought.
bibliography.body: Playful and sophisticated essay arguing that Ibn Turka's system shares structural principles with jazz: systematic but improvisational, rule-governed yet creative, grounded in deep knowledge while allowing freedom. Illustrates how lettrist science is not merely historical artifact but living philosophy.

bibliography.author: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew
bibliography.title: Imperial Talismanic Love: Ibn Turka's Debate of Feast and Fight (1426) as Philosophical Romance and Lettrist Mirror for Timurid Princes
bibliography.card: **Imperial Talismanic Love** — the study of Ibn Turka's *Debate of Feast and Fight* (1426) as both philosophical romance and lettrist mirror for princes. Its opening pages carry the best-documented material in the corpus on **Akhlāṭī as Sultan Barqūq's personal physician**, on Barqūq's resulting interest in the occult sciences, and on Ibn Turka's own place among his courtiers.
bibliography.body:
Takes a single late work — the *Debate of Feast and Fight*, written 1426, in the middle of the years of accusation — and reads it as simultaneously a philosophical romance and a mirror for princes written in lettrist terms. The framing matters for the portal because it shows the science being deployed as political counsel rather than as private metaphysics.

The article is also the source for several of this portal's load-bearing biographical claims about the Cairo years, and for the three-stage periodisation of lettrism from Ibn ʿArabian-Būnian science of the saints, through Mamluk adabization, to neopythagoreanization at the turn of the fifteenth century.

sections.heading: Akhlāṭī and Barqūq, p. 70
sections.summary: Akhlāṭī was summoned to Cairo to serve as **personal physician to Sultan Barqūq**, under whose influence the Mamluk ruler seems to have developed a keen interest in the occult sciences — as his personal library and choice of courtiers, **including Ibn Turka himself**, suggest. Asks whether Barqūq was the first Mamluk sultan to aspire to occult-philosopher-kingship, and so an inspiration for Timurid rivals; answers 'likely so'.

sections.heading: The three stages of lettrism, p. 70
sections.summary: In the 13th century lettrism is the Ibn ʿArabian-Būnian **science of the saints** (*ʿilm al-awliyāʾ*) par excellence; in the 14th it is de-esotericized and adabized through incorporation into the Mamluk literary-political mainstream; and by the turn of the 15th it is **neopythagoreanized** by the occultists who would form the Brethren.

sections.heading: The first major work, p. 70
sections.summary: The *Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-durar*, completed 1404 at the end of the Cairo years, closely tracks high Mamluk Arabic literary culture and timuridizes the Mamluk anthology-as-commentary genre pioneered by Ibn Nubāta (d. 1366) and al-Ṣafadī (d. 1363), both of whom also wrote seminal sword-versus-pen debates.

texts.title: Kitab al-Mafahis
texts.title_transliterated: Kitāb al-Mafāḥīs fī Asrār al-Ḥurūf wa-l-Awfāq
texts.title_translated: Book of Inquiries into the Secrets of Letters and Talismanic Squares
texts.card: **Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ** (Book of Inquiries). Ibn Turka's magnum opus and, in Melvin-Koushki's description, **the first Arabic summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism**. Begun shortly after *Of Letters* and almost certainly at the instance of his patron Iskandar Sulṭān; completed 823/1420, revised and expanded 828/1425. It sets out the fourfold analysis of the letter that is the technical core of his [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist metaphysics]].
texts.body:
## Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ: the first Arabic summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism

**Composition.** Ibn Turka began the *Book of Inquiries* shortly after completing his earlier treatise *Of Letters*, and again almost certainly at the instance of **Iskandar Sulṭān**. He completed it in **823/1420** and revised and expanded it in **828/1425**. Melvin-Koushki calls it the first Arabic summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism and the fullest expression of Ibn Turka's lettrist metaphysics (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

**The fourfold schema.** The *Mafāḥiṣ* massively expands the fourfold schema first proposed in *Of Letters*, treating the meanings of the letters according to their three forms —

- **numerological** (*iḥṣāʾī*)
- **symbological** (*kitābī*)
- **phonological** (*kalāmī*)

— together with a fourth register: the letters **as they are in themselves** (*fī anfusi-hā*). That fourth term is what separates Ibn Turka's project from technique. The first three treat the letter as it is counted, written and spoken; the fourth treats it as a thing with its own being, prior to any of these. A science of letters in that fourth sense is an ontology, not a manual.

**Theological ground.** Lettrist theory of this kind is necessarily predicated on the doctrine of the **uncreatedness of the Qur'an** — if the letters were created artefacts they could not carry the ontological weight placed on them. Ibn Turka accordingly bemoans the contemporary popularity of Zamakhsharī's (d. 538/1144) *Kashshāf*, singling out for censure its failure to recognise the intrinsic ontological majesty of the quranic letters (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66 n.88, citing 'The Quest', 59, 54, 76, 116, 342).

**Transmission.** Over half of Ibn Turka's roughly forty-six known Persian and Arabic works remain in manuscript, the lettrist works most of all, on the assumption that they were the most marginal part of his output. The *Mafāḥiṣ* is the central casualty of that assumption and the principal object of Melvin-Koushki's dissertation, which presents and contextualises it.

## The fourfold schema, unpacked

The technical core of the book is an analysis of the letter in four registers, expanding a
scheme first proposed in the earlier *Of Letters*. The letters are treated according to
their three **forms** —

- **numerological** (*iḥṣāʾī*) — the letter as counted, the [[abjad-numerology|abjad]] value
  and everything computable from it;
- **symbological** (*kitābī*) — the letter as written, its shape, its geometry, its
  disposition on the page;
- **phonological** (*kalāmī*) — the letter as spoken, its sound, its point of articulation,
  its behaviour in recitation;

— and then, in a fourth and separate register, **as they are in themselves**
(*fī anfusi-hā*) (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

The fourth term is what makes the book a work of metaphysics rather than a manual. The
first three treat the letter as it appears to counting, sight and hearing — three modes of
