access. The fourth treats the letter as a being with its own nature prior to any access at
all. A science that stops at the first three is a technique; a science that reaches the
fourth is an ontology, and it is on the fourth that the claim to be the
[[occult-science-universal|only truly universal science]] rests.

## What the book has to presuppose

Lettrist theory of this kind is **necessarily predicated on the doctrine of the
uncreatedness of the Qur'an**. If the letters were created things, they could not be the
principles through which creation is constituted; the argument would invert. Ibn Turka is
alert to this and polices it: he bemoans the contemporary popularity of Zamakhsharī's
(d. 538/1144) *Kashshāf*, singling out for censure its failure to recognise **the intrinsic
ontological majesty of the quranic letters** (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66 n.88, citing
*The Quest*, 54, 59, 76, 116, 342).

That is a revealing target. The *Kashshāf* is a celebrated and widely taught exegesis. To
attack it on this point is to say that the standard way of reading the Qur'an in his own
century had missed what the letters are.

## Where it sits in the oeuvre

The *Mafāḥiṣ* is the summa, and Melvin-Koushki's description of it is precise: **the first
Arabic summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism**, and the fullest expression of Ibn Turka's
lettrist metaphysics (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66). Two points of placement matter.

**Against the *Tamhīd*.** The [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*]] is far better known
in the modern period and is, in the estimation of the author and his contemporaries,
**strictly of secondary importance**. The *Mafāḥiṣ* is the book he thought he had written.
The inversion of their reputations is the central historiographical fact about his
reception.

**Against the chronology.** It was completed in **823/1420 and revised and expanded in
828/1425** — the revision falling in the same window, 827–29/1425–27, in which two-thirds
of the surviving oeuvre was being copied into [[ms-majlis-10196|MS Majlis 10196]], and
immediately before the exile of 1427. The book was being finished and recopied while its
author's position was collapsing.

## The manuscript witness

The best witness is [[ms-majlis-10196|MS Majlis 10196]], and it is unusually good: **the
incipit and explicit of the *Mafāḥiṣ*, folios 52a and 118b, are in Ibn Turka's own hand**.
The copyist was in contact with the author at the opening and the close of this text
specifically. Where a colophon in that codex dates the *Mafāḥiṣ*, the chain of custody is
about as short as this material ever offers.

## Access

Chapter 7 of the dissertation consists largely of **translated sections from the
*Mafāḥiṣ***, and Part 2 supplies editions and translations of five minor lettrist
treatises. For a reader without Arabic that chapter is the closest thing to the book
itself.

## What we do not know

- **There is no critical edition.** The work is known through manuscripts and through
  Melvin-Koushki's translated selections.
- **Whether Iskandar commissioned it** is a judgement — "almost certainly at his instance"
  — not a documented fact.
- **What the 828/1425 revision changed** is not laid out in the sources in hand; we know
  that it was expanded, not how.
- **Whether the colophon dates composition or transcription** is, for much of the codex,
  undecidable.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 54, 59, 76, 116, 342.

texts.title: Treatise on the Barzakh
texts.card: **Risalat al-Barzakh**. Ibn Turka's dedicated treatise on the intermediate realm (barzakh) where causation operates. Expounds the metaphysical framework grounding all lettrist operations: how divine names become manifest in forms, how letters function as operative principles, how human will participates in cosmic causation through knowledge of the barzakh.
texts.body: The Treatise on the Barzakh is Ibn Turka's specialized exposition of the ontological and operative theory of the intermediate realm. Where the Kitab al-Mafahis provides comprehensive systematization of all lettrist sciences, the Barzakh treatise focuses on the metaphysical domain where all operations occur. It establishes: (1) Ontological status of barzakh—it is not merely symbolic or psychological but an actual realm possessing objective reality. (2) The barzakh as causal nexus—all causation flows through the intermediate domain; material effects originate in barzakh-level operations. (3) Human participation—the soul operates in the barzakh; through knowledge of letters and divine names, the will can align with cosmic principles and effect change. (4) Letters as barzakh-entities—letters are primarily barzakh realities; their material expression (ink, stone, parchment) is secondary manifestation. The Barzakh treatise is essential reading for understanding the operational framework underlying all talismanic and lettrist practice.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court, pp. 150–200.

texts.title: Book of Light
texts.card: **Kitab al-Nur** (Book of Light). Ibn Turka's treatise on cosmological doctrines grounded in lettrist and Pythagorean principles. Expounds how divine light manifests through cosmic levels (intelligible, imaginal, sensible), how letters express this cascading illumination, and how human consciousness participates in cosmic light through lettrist gnosis.
texts.body: The Book of Light develops Ibn Turka's cosmological system emphasizing the role of illumination (*nur*) in creation. Drawing on Suhrawardi's Illuminationist philosophy and Ibn Arabi's metaphysics, Ibn Turka presents creation as hierarchical emanation of divine light through progressively dimmer grades. Letters function as vehicles of this light—each letter is a specific frequency of divine illumination. Through [[abjad-numerology|numerical correspondences]] and meditation on letters, consciousness aligns with these cosmic levels and participates in the light-principles governing reality. The Book of Light bridges mystical vision (direct perception of divine light) with systematic cosmology (mathematical and lettrist ordering of creation).
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Being with a Capital B, Ch. 2.

texts.title: Treatise on the Divine Names
texts.card: Ibn Turka's exposition of divine names and their correspondence to 28 letters. Demonstrates integration of Islamic theology with systematic magic.
texts.body: Treatise systematically maps divine names to Arabic letters. Each letter expresses a divine attribute; invoking through its letter accesses that attribute's cosmic power. Bridges Islamic theology with operative magic.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Of Islamic Grammatology.

texts.title: MS Majlis 10196
texts.card: **MS Majlis 10196** — the earliest, most complete and most reliable collection of Ibn Turka's works, copied over the last eight years of his life and three years past his death. **The incipit and explicit of the [[kitab-al-mafahis|Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ]], ff. 52a and 118b, are in the author's own hand.** It is the manuscript on which the dating of the whole oeuvre rests.
texts.body:
## The manuscript that dates everything else

**What it is.** A collection of Ibn Turka's works copied across the last eight years of his life and continuing three years past his death. Melvin-Koushki relies on its colophons wherever possible in establishing when each work was composed, because it is the earliest, most complete and most reliable witness available (*The Quest*, §2.1).

**Why it is unusually good evidence.** The incipit and explicit of the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] — folios 52a and 118b — **are written in Ibn Turka's own hand**. A copyist who could hand the volume to its author for the opening and closing lines was in close contact with him at various points, which lends the colophons elsewhere in the manuscript a credibility that a later copy could not have.

**The limits, stated honestly.** Melvin-Koushki is careful about what the colophons can bear. In many instances it is impossible to tell whether a date records composition or merely transcription. Fully half the manuscript — representing almost two-thirds of the preserved works — was copied between 827–29/1425–27, the period bracketing the exile, so the clustering may reflect a copying campaign rather than a burst of writing. The chronology built on it is a preliminary attempt, and is presented as one.

**Why a game and a portal should care.** Nearly every date in the [[chronology|chronology]] descends from this codex. When an entry here says a work was finished in 823/1420, the chain of custody for that claim runs back to a colophon in MS Majlis 10196, and the honest description of it is *the best available evidence*, not *the record*.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), §2.1 and chronology.

texts.title: Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid
texts.card: **Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid** — a synthesis of Ibn Sīnā, Suhrawardī and Ibn ʿArabī/Qūnavī on absolute being, and **by far the best known of Ibn Turka's works in the modern period**. It is also, in the estimation of the author and his contemporaries, *strictly of secondary importance*. Its fame is the single largest reason his actual project was misread for a century.
texts.body:
## The famous book that got him wrong

**The work.** The *Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid* addresses the doubts of the peripatetics and illuminationists on the topic of absolute being (*al-wujūd al-muṭlaq*), relying primarily on the [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] school tradition as formulated by [[qunavi|Qūnavī]] and [[jandi|Jandī]]. It is a serious and accomplished piece of scholastic metaphysics.

**Its modern career.** It became a staple teaching text in Imami seminary curricula in Iran, probably adopted in the late Qajar period, and Ibn Turka's modern reputation in Iran rests almost exclusively on it. ʿAllāma Ṭabāṭabāʾī celebrates him in *al-Mīzān* as a preeminent synthesizer of peripatetic philosophy and theoretical mysticism; the standard picture places him somewhere between Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī and Mullā Ṣadrā (*The Quest*, 6).

**The problem.** The *Tamhīd* is **bare of any reference to the author's more central lettrist concerns**, and Melvin-Koushki's verdict on its standing is blunt: it is by far the best known of the works in the modern period but strictly of secondary importance in the estimation of the author and his contemporaries. A reputation built on it produces a distorted image of a Sufi-philosopher in the scholastic mode — in short, a mere precursor to the philosophical school of Isfahan.

**Why this matters beyond bibliography.** The irony Melvin-Koushki draws out is exact: the acclaim is *what caused the neglect*. Being celebrated since the nineteenth century as the link between Ibn ʿArabī and Mullā Ṣadrā is precisely what marginalised the [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist]] half of the oeuvre, by abstracting the project from its historical context and robbing it of its animating virtue (*The Quest*, ii). Over half his roughly forty-five works remain in manuscript, the lettrist ones above all, on the assumption that they are the marginal part. The *Tamhīd* is the reason that assumption was ever plausible.

## The mechanism of the distortion

It is worth being exact about *how* a book's fame damages an author's reputation, because
the case is unusually clean.

**Step one: the work enters a curriculum.** The *Tamhīd* became a staple teaching text in
Imami seminary curricula in Iran, probably adopted in the late Qajar period. Curricular
texts are read by everyone in a tradition and become the lens through which their author is
known.

**Step two: the curriculum defines the author.** Ibn Turka's modern reputation in Iran rests
**almost exclusively** on it. ʿAllāma Ṭabāṭabāʾī celebrates him in *al-Mīzān* as a
preeminent synthesizer of peripatetic philosophy and theoretical mysticism.

**Step three: the definition excludes the rest.** Because the *Tamhīd* is **bare of any
reference to the author's more central lettrist concerns**, a reputation built on it has no
place to put the lettrist works. They become, by default, the marginal part of the oeuvre —
and over half the corpus, disproportionately the lettrist half, stayed in manuscript on
exactly that assumption (*The Quest*, ii, 6).

**Step four: the neglect looks like a judgement.** Later scholars, finding the lettrist
works unedited, reasonably infer that specialists had assessed and set them aside. They had
not; they had never looked.

## The readings this produced

Three, all rejected by Melvin-Koushki, and each instructive:

- **Corbin** embraced Ibn Turka warmly as a **standard-issue Shiʿi esotericist** — which at
  least complicated the featureless scholastic picture, but imported a confessional
  assumption the sources do not support.
- **The Iranian seminary consensus** places him between Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī and Mullā Ṣadrā:
  a mystical philosopher, a precursor to the school of Isfahan.
- **Lewisohn**, working from the [[nafsat-al-masdur|apologies]] rather than the *Tamhīd*,
  arrives at an orthodox Sunni Sufi thinker — a different route to the same kind of error,
  since the apologies were produced under duress.

Melvin-Koushki's summary of the net effect is blunt: the de facto scholarly consensus
presents Ibn Turka as a mystical philosopher, **effectively obscuring his explicitly
occultist project** (*The Quest*, 6–7).

## What the book is actually good for

None of this makes the *Tamhīd* a bad book. It addresses the doubts of the peripatetics and
illuminationists on absolute being (*al-wujūd al-muṭlaq*), relying on the
[[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] school as formulated by [[qunavi|Qūnavī]] and [[jandi|Jandī]], and
it is accomplished enough to have held a seminary curriculum for over a century. As
evidence it establishes that Ibn Turka was a fully competent scholastic metaphysician — which
matters, because it means the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] is not the work of someone who
took up occultism for want of the harder discipline.

## What we do not know

- **When it was written**, relative to the lettrist works, is not established in the sources
  in hand — which would settle whether it is early scholastic work or a deliberate
  parallel track.
- **Why he wrote a book with no reference to his central concerns** is not answered.
  Audience, patron, occasion and prudence are all candidates; the sources do not choose.
modern_editions: Āshtiyānī, Sayyid Jalāl al-Dīn, intro. and ed. *Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*. Tehran, 1396/1976.
Javādī Āmulī, ʿAbd Allāh. *Taḥrīr-i Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*. Tehran, 1372 Sh./1993.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), ii, 6.

texts.title: Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr
texts.title_translated: Commentary on the Stringing of Pearls
texts.card: **Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr** — Ibn Turka's first major work, completed in Cairo in 806/1404 at the end of his fifteen years abroad. Formally a commentary on Ibn al-Fāriḍ's *al-Tāʾiyya al-kubrā*, it **timuridizes the Mamluk anthology-as-commentary genre** and is the first such commentary to re-poeticize the Ibn ʿArabī school tradition.
texts.body:
**The work.** Completed toward the end of Ibn Turka's Cairo residence, the *Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr* is an ornate Persian commentary on Ibn al-Fāriḍ's (d. 1235) *al-Tāʾiyya al-kubrā*, a favourite teaching text of the [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] school.

**What is original in it.** Melvin-Koushki shows that it closely tracks high Mamluk Arabic literary culture and effectively **timuridizes the new hybrid Mamluk anthology-as-commentary genre**, pioneered by Ibn Nubāta (d. 1366) and his student al-Ṣafadī (d. 1363) — both of whom also wrote seminal sword-versus-pen debates. It is the first such commentary to effectively **re-poeticize** that tradition, bringing each line of the poem into conjunction with several Persian or Arabic lines of verse, both contemporary and classical (*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70).

**Why it belongs in this portal.** It is evidence about formation rather than doctrine. The man who would later argue that letters are cosmic principles began by writing a book about how verses answer to other verses — and he learned the form in Mamluk Cairo and carried it east. The lettrist project has a literary genealogy as well as a philosophical one.

It is also the base text for Akram Jūdī-Niʿmatī's edition, whose introduction supplies the list of works from which Melvin-Koushki's own annotated catalogue is built (*The Quest*, §2.1).
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), §2.1.

texts.title: Munshaʾāt-i Ṣāʾin-i Turka
texts.card: **Munshaʾāt-i Ṣāʾin-i Turka** — some fifty-eight letters, fragments and notes. The single richest biographical source for Ibn Turka, and the reason we know about his dealings with Timurid amirs, his closeness to [[baysunghur|Bāysunghur]], and his friendly relations with Sufis he criticised in print.
texts.body:
**The collection.** Ibn Turka's correspondence survives as fifty-eight letters, letter fragments and notes. They are written in the highly stylized ornate prose typical of period epistolography, and Melvin-Koushki notes that the formulaic quality is itself informative: the formulas encode the addressee's social or political office and spiritual status, which matters because most of these letters lack identifying headers. In a few cases the information is too scant for more than conjecture about who is being written to (*The Quest*, 135–36).

**What the survey shows.** Frequent dealings with various Timurid amirs, and a close relationship with [[baysunghur|Bāysunghur b. Shāhrukh]] in particular. Friendly relations with prominent Iranian Sufis — Shāh Niʿmat Allāh Valī, [[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], Aḥmad Samarqandī, Ḥasan ʿAṭṭār, Sayyid Muḥammad b. Shaykh Kajujī. Letters written to Sufis and administrative officials alike in hopes of resolving what he calls an intolerable situation.

**The tension it exposes.** These friendships sit oddly beside the criticisms of organised [[sufism|Sufism]] in his written work. Melvin-Koushki reads the discrepancy as informative rather than hypocritical: the first three of those Sufis were great promoters of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] in the face of often hostile reaction, which is the likely point of attraction. He criticised the institution and kept the company.

**A companion collection.** The *Munshaʾāt-i Yazdī* contains eight further items relating to Ibn Turka or his immediate family, and it is there rather than in his own letters that the closeness to [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Yazdī]] is adequately visible: attendance at his teacher's *majālis*, journeys to Herat together, and concern for Ibn Turka's children after their father's death. Only one letter to Yazdī survives in Ibn Turka's own collection, from the first stage of his career in Fars — perhaps the rest were too informal to be thought worth preserving.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 135–36.

texts.title: Nafsat al-Maṣdūr (the Apologies)
texts.date_or_period: Two recensions; the second written 834–35/1431–32 at Herat
texts.card: **Nafsat al-Maṣdūr** — Ibn Turka's apologies, written in self-defence during the tribunals and the exile. The second was composed at Herat during the nine months he spent in weekly attendance at court waiting for his case to be reviewed. They are the most personal thing he wrote and, for exactly that reason, **the least reliable guide to what he actually thought**.
texts.body:
**The works.** The *Nafsat al-Maṣdūr* — 'the breath of one afflicted in the chest' — are Ibn Turka's apologies, written under accusation. The second recension belongs to 834–35/1431–32, the nine months at Herat in weekly attendance at court, waiting on a review of his case that never came; he wrote the *Risāla Iʿtiqādiyya* for [[baysunghur|Bāysunghur]] in the same interval (*The Quest*, chronology).

**The trap they set for readers.** Leonard Lewisohn's article on the apologies takes them as evidence of Ibn Turka's real position and presents him as an orthodox Sunni Sufi thinker. Melvin-Koushki's objection is not that the reading is careless but that the genre will not bear it: the image Ibn Turka presents of himself in the apologies, **produced under great duress**, is hardly reflective of his primary concerns (*The Quest*, 6–7).

This is a general lesson about the sources and worth stating plainly. A defendant's account of his own orthodoxy, written while waiting on a tribunal, is a document about the tribunal. Read as autobiography it produces a man who was never especially interesting; read as forensic rhetoric it shows what an accusation of this kind required a man to say.

**What they are good evidence for.** The mechanics of the charge, the vocabulary available for answering it, and the [[hurufism|distinctions]] he thought would carry weight with [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]] court. That is a great deal — provided nobody mistakes it for the system.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 6–7 and chronology.
Lewisohn, Leonard. Article on Ibn Turka's apologies (cited in *The Quest*, 7).

institutions.name: Isfahan Circle
institutions.card: **Isfahan Circle** (Dayira-yi Isfahan). The intellectual network centered on [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] in late 14th- and early 15th-century Isfahan and Yazd. Members included [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Din Yazdi]] (historian), [[qazizada-rumi|Qazizada Rumi]] (mathematician/astronomer), and other Timurid court scholars. Nexus of [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist]] philosophy, [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], and political-administrative theory. The group represented a self-conscious intellectual project to synthesize Islamic occultism with reason, integrating mysticism, philosophy, and operative science.
institutions.body:
## The Isfahan Circle: Nexus of Timurid Occult Science

The **Isfahan Circle** (c. 1395–1432) was the intellectual and social network that crystallized around [[ibn-turka|Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka]] during his residence in Isfahan and Yazd in the early 15th century. This was not a formal institution with buildings or bylaws, but rather a network of scholars, courtiers, administrators, and practitioners who shared commitment to advancing knowledge of the occult sciences, [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], mathematics, and philosophy within the framework of [[ilm-al-huruf|Islamic intellectual orthodoxy]].

### Core Members

The Circle's most prominent members included:

- **[[ibn-turka|Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka]]** — the intellectual hub, occult philosopher and systematizer of [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]
- **[[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdi]]** — historian and occult theorist; author of the *Ẓafarnāma* (universal history organized by astrological and lettrist principles)
- **[[qazizada-rumi|Qāżīzāda Rūmī]]** — mathematician and astronomer; integrator of mathematical rigor into [[ilm-al-huruf|occult inquiry]]
- **[[saad-al-din-hamuyya|Saad al-Din Hamuyya]]** — (slightly earlier, but cited as predecessor by Ibn Turka) pioneering lettrist theorist

### Intellectual Project

The Isfahan Circle was driven by a unified vision: to demonstrate that the occult sciences—particularly [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], [[abjad-numerology|numerology]], and talismanic practice—constitute a legitimate, rational science encompassing metaphysics, ethics, cosmology, and practice. This project required synthesis:

1. **Theoretical**: Integrating [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysics (via the [[qunavi|Qūnavī]]-Jandī school) with [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]] and peripatetic philosophy
2. **Practical**: Demonstrating operative efficacy—showing that knowledge of letters, numbers, and divine names actually produces effects
3. **Political**: Positioning occult science as essential to statecraft and imperial administration

### Historical Context: The Timurid Court

The Isfahan Circle emerged during the reign of [[shahrukh|Shahrukh]] (r. 1405–1447), grandson of Timur. Shahrukh was a patron of scholars and sought legitimacy through cultural achievement and intellectual advancement. The Timurid court in Isfahan and Samarqand became a magnet for scholars across the Islamic world. Within this milieu, Ibn Turka's circle could flourish—court patronage provided resources, institutional sanction provided protection, and the cosmopolitan court environment created space for intellectual experimentation.

### Transregional Network: The Ikhwan al-Safa Connection

Most significantly, the Isfahan Circle saw itself as part of a larger, transregional network stretching from Anatolia through Isfahan to Cairo and Mamluk Syria. Members referred to themselves cryptically as the *Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ* (Brethren of Purity), invoking the name of the famous 10th-century Brethren while claiming to represent a "new" order. This network included Ottoman scholars in Anatolia, Mamluk court practitioners in Cairo, and Persian philosophers scattered across Timurid lands. The network's coherence lay not in formal organization but in shared commitment to the project of [[ilm-al-huruf|occult science as universal system]].

### Legacy

The Isfahan Circle disbanded with Ibn Turka's death (1432) and the gradual fragmentation of Timurid power. However, its intellectual legacy persisted: the systematization of [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], the integration of [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], and the claim that occultism constitutes rational science became foundational to later Safavid, Ottoman, and European occultist traditions. The Circle's members—especially [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Din Yazdi]] through his *Ẓafarnāma*—achieved considerable influence: their works circulated, were copied, were commented upon. By the early 16th century, as Ottoman and Safavid courts consolidated power, the intellectual project inaugurated by the Isfahan Circle had become canonical.

## Where it sits in a larger structure

The Circle is not self-standing and was never meant to be. The dissertation places it
precisely: Ibn Turka and the members of his Isfahan Circle **may be seen as the eastern arm
of a larger network of intellectuals stretching to Anatolia via Cairo and calling
themselves, cryptically, the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ** (*The Quest*, 2). The
[[new-brethren-purity|New Brethren]] entry treats the network; this entry treats its
Iranian node.

The word **cryptically** is doing work. They took the name of the tenth-century Basran
encyclopedists — a name with its own reputation, some of it Ismāʿīlī — without announcing
what they meant by it. A borrowed name is a claim of succession and a partial concealment
at once, which is a fair description of the whole enterprise.

## The schoolroom underneath the circle

The most surprising thing the corpus yields about this group is that its two principal
minds had been in the same classroom for twenty-five years. Ibn Turka studied under his
elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] for the first twenty-five years of his life
**along with [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]** (*The Quest*, 41 n.17).

That reorganises the Circle's intellectual history. The lettrist and the astronomer are not
specialists who converged at a Timurid court to compare notes; they are schoolfellows who
divided a shared inheritance between them. Ṣadr al-Dīn taught only the outward sciences,
deeming it too dangerous to delve into esoteric matters in public — and his two pupils then
spent their careers on the two disciplines by which the hidden order of things might be made
calculable. They died in the same year, 835/1432.

## What each member contributed

- **Ibn Turka** — the [[ilm-al-huruf|theory]], and the claim that it is universal.
- **[[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]** — mathematical astronomy, and, as second director of
  the [[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand Observatory]], the institutional bridge between the
  letter science and the star science.
- **[[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdī]]** — not a peer but Ibn Turka's **disciple
  and closest associate**, who accompanied him from Samarkand to Cairo around 795/1393,
  attended his *majālis*, travelled with him to Herat, and cared for his children after his
  death (*The Quest*, 135–36). He applied the framework to history and to the defence of
  divination.

## The political weather

The Circle formed and worked under conditions the entry should name. [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]]
abrogated *yasa* law in favour of the sharīʿa in 813/1411 and closed the taverns; the same
ruler destroyed [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] in 817/1414, exonerated Ibn Turka in
825/1422, and exiled him in 1427. A circle of occult philosophers operating inside a court
that had refounded its legitimacy on public piety is not a comfortable arrangement, and the
tribunals were its predictable expression.

## What we do not know

- **Membership is not a list.** The Circle is a modern historiographical construct built
  from correspondence and association, not an institution with a roll.
- **Whether it had a meeting place, a rule, or a formal name** among its members is not
  attested; the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ designation is cryptic by nature.
- **How far its members agreed** is largely unrecoverable — we have Ibn Turka's system in
  detail and much less of the others' on the same questions.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Occult Court: Magic, Medicine, and Mathematics in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth-Century Isfahan*. Boston: BRILL, 2025.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 20–50.

institutions.name: New Brethren of Purity
institutions.card: **Ikhwan al-Safa al-Jadid** (The New Brethren of Purity). Transregional network of late 14th- and 15th-century scholars, occultists, and courtiers claiming succession to the 10th-century Brethren of Purity. Members included [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]], [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlati]], [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Din Yazdi]], and figures across Ottoman, Mamluk, and Persian courts. United by commitment to [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], [[abjad-numerology|numerology]], and the integration of occult sciences with [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean philosophy]]. Represented a self-conscious intellectual movement to establish occultism as legitimate, rational universal science.
institutions.body:
## Ikhwan al-Safa al-Jadid: The New Brethren of Purity

The **New Brethren of Purity** (Ikhwan al-Safa al-Jadid) was a transregional network of scholars and practitioners spanning three major power centers—Ottoman Anatolia, Mamluk Egypt/Syria, and Timurid Persia—in the late 14th and 15th centuries. They invoked the name of the legendary 10th-century Brethren of Purity (*Ikhwan al-Safa*), but understood themselves as a *new* order inaugurating a fresh era of occult science.

### Network Structure

Unlike formal institutions, the New Brethren functioned as a loose confederation bound by shared intellectual commitments rather than hierarchy or bylaws. Key nodes included:
- **Isfahan Circle** ([[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]], [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Din Yazdi]], [[qazizada-rumi|Qazizada Rumi]])
- **Cairo/Mamluk court** ([[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Sayyid Husayn Akhlati]], Ottoman and Mamluk occultists)
- **Anatolian scholars** (Ottoman court philosophers and talismanic practitioners)

### Core Project

The New Brethren were united by a single grand project: to establish that [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], [[abjad-numerology|numerology]], [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], and [[divine-names|divine-names doctrine]] constitute a comprehensive, rational science encompassing metaphysics, ethics, cosmology, and operative practice. This was not mysticism in the Sufi sense but *rational occultism*—grounded in logic, mathematics, and philosophical rigor.

### Historical Significance

Melvin-Koushki's research demonstrates that the New Brethren were not marginal occultists but central intellectual figures in their respective courts, commanding patronage, commanding audiences, and exerting real influence over political and administrative thought. They succeeded in their project: by the early 16th century, their intellectual synthesis had become canonical in Ottoman and Safavid philosophy.

The New Brethren represent a crucial moment in global intellectual history—when Islamic occult philosophy achieved systematic articulation, international coordination, and institutional legitimacy, rivaling and arguably exceeding contemporary European and Chinese philosophical achievements.

## Who established that this network existed

The network is not a category the sources hand over ready-made; it is a modern reconstruction, and the portal should say whose. Its existence was **posited by İhsan Fazlıoğlu in a 1996 article** on the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ and [[bistami|ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī]] in early Ottoman intellectual life. Melvin-Koushki states that his own understanding of late medieval Islamic occult philosophy is **dependent on the ongoing research of Cornell Fleischer** and his Chicago Circle into the cognate Ottoman projects (*The Quest*, ch. 1 nn. 87–88).

The two branches are described as **largely coterminous both logistically and conceptually**, so work on either has vital bearing on the whole complex. The [[isfahan-circle|Isfahan Circle]] is the eastern arm of something that reached Anatolia through Cairo, and reading the Iranian half alone produces a partial picture by construction.

One comparative fact is worth sitting with: Melvin-Koushki calls the Ottoman projects **cognate and more successful**. The same inheritance from the same teacher flourished at one end of the network and ended in tribunals at the other.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The New Brethren of Purity: Occult Science and Statecraft in the Islamic World*. Boston: BRILL, 2019.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Occult Court: Magic, Medicine, and Mathematics in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth-Century Isfahan*. Boston: BRILL, 2025.
Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 2 and ch. 1 nn. 87–88.
Fazlıoğlu, İhsan (1996); Fleischer, Cornell, *A Mediterranean Apocalypse* (in progress).

institutions.name: The Samarkand Observatory
institutions.card: **The Samarkand Observatory**, founded by [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] in 1420 around a meridian arc of unprecedented scale. Its *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* was the most accurate star table in the world for two centuries. Melvin-Koushki's argument places it inside Ibn Turka's story rather than beside it: the mathematization of astronomy achieved here and the [[neoplatonism|mathematicalization of the occult sciences]] are the same movement, and have been studied in isolation only by accident of modern disciplinary boundaries.
institutions.body:
## The Samarkand Observatory

**The institution.** [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] broke ground in 1420 on what became the largest astronomical instrument on earth: a meridian arc sunk into bedrock, housed in a three-storey building, staffed by the best mathematical astronomers of the age — Qāḍīzāda Rūmī among them, and later Jamshīd al-Kāshī and ʿAlī Qushjī. The *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* it produced remained the most accurate star catalogue in the world for roughly two centuries.

**Why it belongs to this portal.** The conventional account treats Samarkand as a triumph of exact science and Timurid occultism as a separate, embarrassing phenomenon. Melvin-Koushki's thesis denies the separation. He argues that the mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and sanctification of occultism in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran is *the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context* for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy by the members of the Samarkand Observatory — processes which, he notes, have heretofore been studied in atomistic isolation (*Powers of One*, 1).

The observatory and the [[kitab-al-mafahis|Book of Inquiries]] were begun in the same year, 1420, a few hundred miles apart, by men working out the same conviction: that a science earns its standing by becoming mathematical. [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]] worked at both ends of it.

**The end.** Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449 and the observatory was abandoned and dismantled not long after; its foundations were not rediscovered until 1908. The tables outlived the building, and reached Mughal India, where Shāhjahān's *Zīj-i Shāhjahānī* updated them behind the first thoroughly **lettrist** preface in the Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition (*Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599).
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Timurid-Mughal Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599.
Blake, Stephen P. *Astronomy and Astrology in the Islamic World*, ch. 6.

timeline_events.title: Ibn Turka born in Isfahan
timeline_events.card: Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī is born into an established Isfahani scholarly family. His father Afżal al-Dīn and elder brother Ṣadr al-Dīn are both men of the religious sciences; the brother will be appointed *qāḍī* and will teach him for his first twenty-five years.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fażl Allāh Astarābādī in Isfahan
timeline_events.card: The future founder of the Ḥurūfiyya arrives in Isfahan and becomes famous as an interpreter of dreams. Ibn Turka's father and elder brother both consult him — a documented family contact that prosecutors would still be able to use sixty years later.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Studies under his brother, with Qāḍīzāda Rūmī
timeline_events.card: For the first twenty-five years of his life Ibn Turka studies under his elder brother Ṣadr al-Dīn — **alongside Qāḍīzāda Rūmī**, the future director of the Samarkand Observatory. He later remarks that his brother taught nothing beyond the outward sciences.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Leaves Samarkand for Mecca and Cairo, with Yazdī
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka departs for the Ḥijāz and then Cairo. **Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdī accompanies him** — the disciple is with him from the beginning of the formative journey, not acquired later at court.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fifteen years abroad: study under Akhlāṭī in Cairo
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka studies under Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī, Sirāj al-Dīn al-Bulqīnī and others, remaining abroad fifteen years. Akhlāṭī — summoned to Cairo as personal physician to Sultan Barqūq — is the pivot of the network that will call itself the New Brethren of Purity.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fażl Allāh Astarābādī executed
timeline_events.card: The founder of the Ḥurūfiyya is executed at the fortress of Alinjaq by Mīrānshāh b. Tīmūr. The movement he leaves behind becomes the heresy from which Ibn Turka's own science must afterwards be distinguished.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Akhlāṭī dies in Cairo
timeline_events.card: The master of the Cairo circle dies. Ibn Turka will present himself thereafter as the systematizer of Akhlāṭī's teachings, and was received as such by the later lettrist tradition.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Completes the Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr
timeline_events.card: His first major work, in Persian: a commentary on Ibn al-Fāriḍ's *al-Tāʾiyya al-kubrā*, a favourite teaching text of the Ibn ʿArabī school. It timuridizes the Mamluk anthology-as-commentary genre and is the first such commentary to re-poeticize that tradition.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Tīmūr dies at Utrar
timeline_events.card: The founder of the dynasty dies on campaign, opening the succession struggle out of which Shāhrukh will emerge and within which Ibn Turka's patrons will rise and fall.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Returns to Isfahan and takes up teaching
timeline_events.card: After fifteen years abroad Ibn Turka comes home and begins to teach. The Cairo formation is complete; the Persian career begins.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: At Pīr-Muḥammad's court in Shiraz
timeline_events.card: A first Timurid attachment, to the court of Pīr-Muḥammad b. ʿUmar-Shaykh — cut short when Pīr-Muḥammad is murdered in 812/1409 and his brother Iskandar rises to power in Fars.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Appointed qāḍī at Iskandar Sulṭān's court
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka joins the court of Iskandar Sulṭān, appointed *qāḍī* and teacher. Iskandar commissions *Of Letters* and, shortly after, the Book of Inquiries — the patronage that produces his central work.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Shāhrukh abrogates yasa law for the sharīʿa
timeline_events.card: Shāhrukh declares the abrogation of Mongol *yasa* law, enforces the sharīʿa and closes the taverns. Timurid legitimacy is refounded on religious rather than steppe grounds — and the ground on which an occult philosopher will be judged shifts with it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Completes the Sharḥ Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam
timeline_events.card: A commentary on Ibn ʿArabī's *Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam*, completed in the year he travels to the Ḥijāz and invites Sharaf al-Dīn to join him. A corrected version follows in 817/1415.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Iskandar takes Isfahan and builds a brilliant court
timeline_events.card: Iskandar Sulṭān establishes at Isfahan one of the most lavishly bookish and most astrologically preoccupied courts of the age. Ibn Turka is attached to it — then moves back to Shiraz under harassment by envious individuals, putting forward his protégé Sharaf al-Dīn Yaʿqūb to replace him as *qāḍī*.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Shāhrukh destroys Iskandar Sulṭān
timeline_events.card: Shāhrukh marches against Iskandar in Iraq. Iskandar flees, is captured and blinded, and is executed afterwards; Ibrāhīm Sulṭān is installed in his place. Ibn Turka's first patron is destroyed by the ruler he must now live under.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Writes the Risālat al-Ḥurūf in Shiraz
timeline_events.card: *Of Letters*, written for Iskandar Sulṭān — the treatise that first proposes the fourfold analysis of the letter which the Book of Inquiries will expand.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Attempts to retire from public life
timeline_events.card: For eight years after Iskandar's fall Ibn Turka tries to withdraw. It is the most productive stretch of his life: the Book of Inquiries is completed inside it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Completes the Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ
timeline_events.card: The Book of Inquiries is finished — the first Arabic summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism. It is revised and expanded in 828/1425. **Ulugh Beg breaks ground on the Samarkand Observatory the same year**: two foundations laid in one year, one in stone and one on paper.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Ulugh Beg founds the Samarkand Observatory
timeline_events.card: Ground is broken on the largest astronomical instrument on earth. Melvin-Koushki argues that the mathematicalization of the occult sciences is the immediate context for the mathematization of astronomy achieved here — the two are one movement, not two.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Accused of Sufi bias; clears his name at Herat
timeline_events.card: His opponents go to Shāhrukh's court and accuse him of Sufi bias. Ibn Turka travels to Herat to answer them in person, **gains Shāhrukh's favour, and is given the judgeship of Yazd**. The first tribunal, and he wins it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Exiled from Herat with Qāsim-i Anvār
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka is expelled alongside Qāsim-i Anvār, his charismatic associate from the Cairo years, over suspect connections — the official excuse being a putative Ḥurūfī link. The stated charge and the operative reason are not the same.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** In 1427 Ibn Turka was expelled from Herat together with
[[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], his charismatic associate from the Cairo years. The
dissertation is specific about the mechanism: they were exiled **for suspect connections**,
though it was Qāsim's **putative connection with the Ḥurūfīs that provided the official
excuse** (*The Quest*, 456 n.16).

**The distinction that matters.** The stated charge and the operative reason are not the
same, and the sources let us see the gap. The operative worry was association — Qāsim was a
propagandist of the Ṣafaviyya order and was apparently claimed by Ismāʿīlīs as one of their
own, at a moment when that was dangerous: [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] had attempted a purge of
Ismāʿīlīs in Quhistan in 1415. The [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] label was the charge that would
carry in court.

**Why the label was available.** Because it was not baseless in the family's case. Ḥurūfī
sources record that Ibn Turka's father Afżal al-Dīn and his elder brother
[[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] had consulted Fażl Allāh Astarābādī during his Isfahan
residence, presenting dreams for interpretation. Melvin-Koushki cautions that this implies
no Ḥurūfī inclination and that the story's hagiographical purpose is to show Fażl Allāh's
standing *before* his messianic turn — but the episode is on the record and a prosecutor
could reach it.

**What it cost.** The exile ends the settled portion of the career. What follows is the
sequence the [[chronology|chronology]] records: a fruitless attempt at a hearing in Simnan
around 833/1429, a winter at Natanz, a promise of reinstatement at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa around
834/1430, and then nine months of weekly attendance at court in Herat waiting for a review
that had not come when he died in 835/1432.

**The irony of the timing.** In 835/1432, the year of his death, there were **Ḥurūfī
uprisings in Isfahan and Tabriz**. The charge that had removed him five years earlier
acquired, at exactly the wrong moment, the appearance of foresight.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Muḥammad al-Jazarī, his powerful opponent, dies
timeline_events.card: The death in Herat of the man the chronology names as Ibn Turka's powerful opponent. It does not restore him: the machinery of the case outlives its instigator.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fruitless attempt to obtain a hearing at Simnan
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka tries and fails to get in front of Shāhrukh. The exile is now a matter of waiting on access.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Winters at Natanz and writes for his son
timeline_events.card: He sends for his family and, while there, writes the *Kitāb al-Manāhij* for his son Muḥammad. The transmission problem has become domestic.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: A promise of reinstatement at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka finally obtains a hearing at Shāhrukh's camp and **receives a promise of reinstatement**. It is the high point of the last years and it is only a promise.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Nine months in weekly attendance, waiting on a case review
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka travels to Herat and for nine months attends court weekly, waiting for his case to be reviewed. In that interval he writes *Nafsat al-Maṣdūr II* and the *Risāla Iʿtiqādiyya* for Bāysunghur. The review does not come.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Having obtained a promise of reinstatement at Shāhrukh's camp at Ṣāʾin
Qalʿa near Sultaniyya around 834/1430, Ibn Turka travelled to Herat. There, across
834–35/1431–32, he was **for nine months in weekly attendance at court waiting for the
review of his case** (*The Quest*, chronology). The review did not come. He died at Herat
in 835/1432.

**What he did with the time.** He wrote. The chronology places two works in this interval:
the second recension of the [[nafsat-al-masdur|*Nafsat al-Maṣdūr*]] — the apologies — and
the *Risāla Iʿtiqādiyya*, composed **for [[baysunghur|Bāysunghur]]**. Both are documents of
a man arguing for himself: one a defence, one a statement of belief addressed to the
Timurid prince he had been closest to.

**How to read the apology written here.** With care. Melvin-Koushki's warning about the
genre applies with maximum force to a text produced in these conditions: the self-image Ibn
Turka presents in the apologies, **produced under great duress**, is hardly reflective of
his primary concerns (*The Quest*, 6–7). Leonard Lewisohn's reading of him as an orthodox
Sunni Sufi thinker rests on exactly this material. A creed written in the ninth month of
waiting on a tribunal is evidence about the tribunal.

**Why the shape of it matters.** This is not a dramatic ending. There is no verdict, no
condemnation, no scene. There is an old man attending court once a week for the better part
of a year because a promise had been made, and then there is a death. The most consequential
occult philosopher of Timurid Iran spent his last year in an antechamber.

**The rhyme with Samarkand.** [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] — the patron whose programme was his
own programme — had seventeen years left. The [[samarkand-observatory|observatory]] was
running. The patronage that would have made sense of the whole career was three weeks' ride
away and never arrived, for the same reason the case review never arrived: not refusal, but
a court's ordinary capacity to defer.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Ḥurūfī uprisings at Isfahan and Tabriz
timeline_events.card: In the year of his death the movement he had spent a career being distinguished from rises in his own city. The charge that exiled him is, at exactly the wrong moment, politically vindicated.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Dies at Herat
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka dies still waiting on the review of his case. Ulugh Beg — the patron whose programme was his own — has seventeen years left; the Samarkand tables will carry an unsigned debt to the letter science for two centuries.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: MS Majlis 10196 copied, partly in the author's hand
timeline_events.card: The earliest, most complete and most reliable collection of Ibn Turka's works, copied over the last eight years of his life and three years past his death. **The incipit and explicit of the Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ, ff. 52a and 118b, are in Ibn Turka's own hand** — the copyist was in close contact with the author. It is the basis for dating most of the oeuvre.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: A Saturn–Jupiter conjunction in Scorpio
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka holds that his own generation's evolution was heralded by a portentous celestial conjunction — **likely Saturn–Jupiter in Scorpio in 767/1365**. His generation, poised on the edge of history and encompassing all that went before, is therefore the best generation, and the late 8th/14th century the **beginning of a golden age in which the prophetic legacy transmitted by the Imams and the ancients would be actualized**. Melvin-Koushki flags his own uncertainty about which conjunction is meant.
timeline_events.body:
**What the claim is.** Ibn Turka holds that the evolution of his own generation was heralded
by a portentous celestial conjunction. Melvin-Koushki identifies it as *likely* the
Saturn–Jupiter conjunction in Scorpio of 767/1365, while stating in a footnote that he is
**not entirely sure which conjunction Ibn Turka has in mind** (*The Quest*, 21 n.8). The
uncertainty is preserved here because it is the scholar's own.

**Why a conjunction.** Saturn–Jupiter conjunctions are the backbone of Islamicate
historical astrology. They recur roughly every twenty years, shift triplicity every couple
of centuries, and complete a full cycle in something under a millennium; the tradition
reads the greater ones as marking dynastic and religious turning points. To claim one as
the herald of your own generation is to place that generation in a cycle of world-history,
not merely to note an omen.

**The claim it licenses.** From the portent Ibn Turka draws a strong conclusion: his
generation, **poised on the edge of history and encompassing all that went before, is
therefore the best generation**, and the late 8th/14th century is **the beginning of a
golden age in which the prophetic legacy transmitted by the Imams and the ancients would be
actualized** (*The Quest*, 21).

**Why this is not Ḥurūfism.** The structure is millenarian, and Melvin-Koushki grants
without hesitation that Ibn Turka is a profoundly millenarian thinker by any standard. What
keeps it inside orthodoxy is the object: a golden age of **knowledge**, in which what the
Imams and ancients already transmitted becomes fully actual — not a new revelation. The
insistence on the binding finality of the dispensation given through Muḥammad is what
separates this from the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] claim (*The Quest*, 456).

**Consequences.** Almost everything programmatic in the career follows from this dating.
If the golden age has begun, then the occult knowledge of the ancients is due to be made
manifest, and a man who systematises it is not an antiquarian but a participant in a
scheduled event. The urgency of the project, and its confidence, are both downstream of a
conjunction.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 21 and n.8

timeline_events.title: The reign of Tīmūr
timeline_events.card: Tīmūr rules the empire into which Ibn Turka is born and which will employ, elevate and eventually prosecute him. It is Tīmūr who appoints his brother Ṣadr al-Dīn *qāḍī* in Samarkand, establishing the judgeship as a Turka family office.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 34

timeline_events.title: The reign of Sultan Barqūq at Cairo
timeline_events.card: Al-Malik al-Ẓāhir Barqūq rules the Mamluk sultanate. **Akhlāṭī serves as his personal physician-alchemist**, and under that influence Barqūq develops a keen interest in the occult sciences — evidenced by his personal library and his choice of courtiers, Ibn Turka among them. Melvin-Koushki asks whether he was the first Mamluk sultan to aspire to occult-philosopher-kingship, and answers: likely so.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 6

timeline_events.title: Ibn Khaldūn settles in Cairo
timeline_events.card: Ibn Khaldūn lives in Cairo from 785/1383 until his death in 808/1406 — overlapping the years Ibn Turka and Yazdī spent there. Melvin-Koushki notes that **the two historians possibly met**: Yazdī spent at least part of 795–810/1393–1408 in the city with Ibn Turka. The most formidable critic of the occult sciences and their most consequential defender may have been in the same rooms.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 37

timeline_events.title: Ibn Khaldūn's Damascus interviews with Tīmūr
timeline_events.card: At the famous Damascus interviews, Ibn Khaldūn — the age's leading anti-occultist — attempts, in Melvin-Koushki's reading, **to palm himself off as a seasoned occultist**. The hypocrisy is instructive about how much occult competence was worth in front of a conqueror.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *In Defense of Geomancy*, 36

timeline_events.title: Akhlāṭī as heir of al-Būnī and Ibn ʿArabī
timeline_events.card: Melvin-Koushki characterises Akhlāṭī as the **conscious heir of both al-Būnī and Ibn ʿArabī**, and master to the most important occult philosophers of the following generation. The two streams the portal treats separately — operative talismanic lettrism and Akbarian metaphysics — are joined in one teacher before Ibn Turka inherits them.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 6

timeline_events.title: Iskandar Sulṭān rules Fars
timeline_events.card: Iskandar Sulṭān — grandson of Tīmūr, ruler of Fars and contender with his uncle Shāhrukh for control of Iran — is described by Melvin-Koushki as **Ibn Turka's first and most important patron**.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 34

timeline_events.title: The eschatological-absolutism experiment
timeline_events.card: Melvin-Koushki devotes a study to Mīrzā Iskandar, Shāh Niʿmatullāh Valī and Sayyid Sharīf Jurjānī in 815/1412 as an experiment with eschatological absolutism, and draws a sharp conclusion: **if the rise of absolutist politics is a benchmark for early modernity, then in 816/1412 Shāhrukh was the last medieval Islamic ruler and Mīrzā Iskandar the first early modern absolutist sovereign.** Ibn Turka is attached to the court where this happens.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Imperial Talismanic Love*, 16, 21

timeline_events.title: The reign of Shāhrukh
timeline_events.card: Shāhrukh rules for thirty-eight years, spanning almost the whole of Ibn Turka's Persian career — the patron who received him back into favour in 825/1422 and the court that exiled him in 1427.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 34

timeline_events.title: The judgeship of Isfahan becomes a Turka family office
timeline_events.card: Tīmūr appoints Ibn Turka's elder brother **Ṣadr al-Dīn** as *qāḍī* in Samarkand, establishing the office to the Turka family. The judgeship of Isfahan that Iskandar later installs Ibn Turka in — and that the tribunals take from him — is a **hereditary** family possession dating to the founding of the dynasty.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Tīmūr appointed Ibn Turka's elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr
al-Dīn]] as *qāḍī* in Samarkand, and in doing so **established the office to the Turka
family**. When [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] later installed Ibn Turka as *qāḍī* of
Isfahan, he was presumably filling a post the family already held by right
(*The Quest*, §3.1).

**Why this reframes the career.** It changes what the tribunals were taking. Read without
this fact, Ibn Turka is a scholar who obtained a good appointment and later lost it through
controversy. Read with it, he is the holder of **a hereditary family office granted at the
founding of the dynasty**, and the accusations of the 1420s are an attempt to strip a
lineage of a possession, not merely to remove an individual from a job.

**The precise office.** Melvin-Koushki describes him as **Shāfiʿī chief judge of Isfahan and
Yazd** (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 13) — a senior magistracy, in a named legal school,
across two cities. This is a full working career in its own right. Everything in the
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] was written around it.

**What it explains about the opposition.** Rival colleagues engineered the inquisitions,
and a hereditary judgeship is exactly the kind of thing colleagues covet. The chronology
notes that he had already moved back to Shiraz once, in 815–17/1412–14, **due to harassment
by envious individuals**, putting forward his protégé Sharaf al-Dīn Yaʿqūb to replace him as
*qāḍī*. The pattern of professional envy is attested a decade before the tribunals.

**What we do not know.** Whether the Isfahan judgeship was formally the same grant as the
Samarkand one, or a family claim honoured by a later prince, is not spelled out in the
sources in hand.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), §3.1

timeline_events.title: Ten children; two sons known by name
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka states that he had **ten children — three sons and seven daughters**. Only two sons are known by name: **Jamāl al-Dīn Muḥammad**, for whom he wrote his manual of logic the *K. al-Manāhij*, and **Najīb al-Dīn Ḥabīb Allāh**, who appears to have written a brief lettrist treatise of his own, the *Qavāʿid-i Jafr-i Jāmiʿ*. The science stayed in the family for at least one generation.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 41

timeline_events.title: Shāfiʿī chief judge of Isfahan and Yazd
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka's office is described precisely by Melvin-Koushki as **Shāfiʿī chief judge of Isfahan and Yazd** — a working senior magistracy in two cities, in a named legal school. The occult philosophy was written by a man with a full-time judicial day job.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 13

timeline_events.title: Makes mortal enemies at the Cairo court
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka launches his writing career during the fifteen-year Cairo tenure, where he trains in law, Arabic letters and occult science — **and makes mortal enemies at court**. The opposition that culminates in the tribunals of the 1420s begins in Egypt, decades before it bears fruit.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 5

timeline_events.title: Qāḍīzāda Rūmī dies
timeline_events.card: The second director of Ulugh Beg's observatory dies **in the same year as Ibn Turka**. The two had studied together under Ibn Turka's brother for twenty-five years and had divided the work between the stars and the letters; they leave it in the same season.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 41

timeline_events.title: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī dies
timeline_events.card: The Ottoman arm of the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ network outlives its Iranian counterpart by twenty-two years. Bisṭāmī and Ibn Turka were both heirs of Akhlāṭī pursuing the same universalist lettrist project; Melvin-Koushki judges the Ottoman version **more successful**.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 2

timeline_events.title: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ network is identified by modern scholarship
timeline_events.card: İhsan Fazlıoğlu posits the existence of the fifteenth-century Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ network in a 1996 article; Cornell Fleischer and his Chicago Circle develop the Ottoman side. Melvin-Koushki's account of the Isfahan Circle is explicitly dependent on that work — the two branches are **largely coterminous**, and neither can be read alone.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), ch. 1 nn. 87–88

timeline_events.title: The Book of Inquiries revised and expanded
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka returns to the summa five years after finishing it and expands it — in the same period, 827–29/1425–27, in which two-thirds of the surviving oeuvre was being copied into MS Majlis 10196. The revision belongs to the years immediately before the exile.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66
